name: Grade 10
theme: The Church: history, mission and the Paschal Mystery lived

lessons.title: Christ founds the Church
lessons.idea: Jesus founded the Church by preaching the Kingdom, gathering disciples, choosing the Twelve, giving Peter the keys, instituting the Eucharist and sending the apostles on mission. The Church is at once a visible society and a spiritual communion.
lessons.question: What evidence shows Jesus founded a Church?
lessons.activity: “Founding evidence” (35 min). Students gather founding signs from the Gospels: the call of the Twelve (Mark 3:13–19), the keys (Matthew 16:13–20), the power to bind and loose (Matthew 18:18), the Eucharist (Luke 22:19), the commission (Matthew 28:16–20), the gift of the Spirit (John 20:21–23). Place them on a timeline and add what each shows about structure.
teach: The Church’s origin is Christ’s own work: his preaching, the call of the Twelve, the Eucharist, the Cross and the outpouring of the Spirit (CCC 758–766). She is “born from the pierced side of Christ” (CCC 766).
Matthew 16:13–20: Peter’s confession, the rock, the keys (CCC 551–553). Matthew 28:16–20: the Great Commission and the promise “I am with you always” (CCC 861).
The Church is “one complex reality” comprised of a human and a divine element (CCC 771; Lumen Gentium 8). She is a visible society and a spiritual community.
Respond to the claim “Jesus preached the Kingdom, not the Church” by showing that the Kingdom begins in the Church (CCC 541, 763–769).
talk: What evidence shows Jesus founded a community?
What is the role of the Twelve?
Why does the Church need both structure and Spirit?
quiz: Which New Testament action most directly shows Jesus founding a community with structure?|Choosing the Twelve and giving Peter the keys (Matthew 16:18–19; Mark 3:13–19)|Teaching in parables|Healing the sick|Fasting forty days|0|CCC 551–553.

The Church is “born from the pierced side of Christ” because…|Blood and water from his side are signs of the Eucharist and Baptism (CCC 766)|It was built by Constantine|It began at Nicaea|The apostles said so|0|CCC 766; John 19:34.
Which description of the Church fits the Catechism?|A club|A purely human institution|One complex reality with a human and a divine element (CCC 771)|Invisible only|2|CCC 770–771.
lessons.life: Read Matthew 16 and Acts 2 and make a two-column note: Christ’s intention / Pentecost.
lessons.saint: Andrew: the first to be called, who kept bringing people to Jesus.
misc: “Jesus never meant to found an organization.”
lessons.mem: “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If a movement lasted 2,000 years, what must have been built into it at the start?” Make a list: leaders, a mission, a way of worship, a way to hand it on.
lessons.assess: Ask students to list four New Testament actions of Jesus that show he founded a Church.

script.open: Put the question on the board: “Did Jesus found a church, or did the Church just happen?” Ask students to take a side, then say, “We will look at the evidence like historians.”
teach: Say: “Some historians and many people today say that Jesus never meant to start an institution, only to preach the Kingdom, and that the Church was an invention after his death. The Catholic Church says Jesus intended a community with structure, authority and continuity. The evidence from the Gospels: Jesus gathered disciples and chose the Twelve, ‘to be with him and to be sent out.’ Twelve, as in the twelve tribes: he was constituting a renewed Israel (Mark 3:13-19). He gave them a mission, a share in his authority, and a promise.”

Say: “Key texts. Matthew 16:18-19: ‘You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church’; the word ‘ekklesia’ (assembly, church) is used by Jesus himself. The keys, binding and loosing. Matthew 18:17-18: the community has authority to settle disputes. John 21:15-17: ‘Feed my lambs… tend my sheep.’ Luke 22:19: ‘Do this in remembrance of me,’ the institution of a continuing ritual. John 20:21-23: ‘As the Father has sent me, even so I send you,’ with power to forgive sins. Matthew 28:19-20: the commission to baptize and teach all nations ‘to the close of the age,’ which implies a community that will last long after the apostles die.”

Say: “The Church emerges at Pentecost, but is prepared throughout Jesus’ life. Vatican II says: ‘The Lord Jesus inaugurated his Church by preaching the Good News.’ (LG 5) The Catechism describes stages: prepared in the Old Testament, founded by Jesus, revealed by the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, and to be completed in glory. The Church is not a human invention but a gift. Some critics point out that Jesus expected the Kingdom soon. The Church responds that the Kingdom is both present and future, and that the Church is its seed. Peter’s role is also shown by the early record: he is first among the Twelve in every list, speaks first at Pentecost, and presides at the Council of Jerusalem.”
ask: What did Jesus do to found the Church? (Chose the Twelve, gave them authority and a mission, and promised to be with them.)
What word does Jesus himself use in Matthew 16:18? (Church, ekklesia.)
How does the Church describe her origin? (Prepared in the Old Testament, founded by Christ, revealed at Pentecost.)
practice: Build a case file with six claims: Jesus chose the Twelve, gave Peter a special role, gave authority to bind and loose, instituted the Eucharist, commissioned the disciples, promised to remain.
For each, write the Bible verse and how you would argue it.
Rate which is strongest and which weakest.
Write a short paragraph answering a skeptic.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, you built your Church on the rock. Keep us faithful.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Whom could you bring to Jesus, as Andrew did?”

tryit: Build the case that Jesus founded a community.
Cite one text for each claim.
Rate which is strongest.
lessons.saintStory:
Andrew was a fisherman from Bethsaida, on the Sea of Galilee, who had been a disciple of John the Baptist. When John pointed to Jesus and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God,” Andrew followed, spent the day with Jesus, and then went looking for his brother Simon. “We have found the Messiah.” He brought Simon to Jesus. That is why the Eastern Churches call Andrew the “First-called.”
He appears at three other moments, and each time he brings someone. Before the feeding of the five thousand, it was Andrew who pointed to a boy with five barley loaves and two fish: “What are they among so many?” When some Greeks wanted to see Jesus, they went to Philip, who went to Andrew, and the two of them brought them to Jesus.
Tradition says he preached in Greece and Asia Minor and was crucified at Patras on an X-shaped cross. He is patron of Scotland, Russia and Greece. He was a man who was never the leader, but whose work was to introduce others to Christ.

lessons.title: The Church as mystery and sacrament
lessons.idea: Vatican II calls the Church “a kind of sacrament,” a sign and instrument of communion with God and of the unity of the human race. Like the sacraments, the Church is visible and invisible at once, a mystery rooted in the Trinity.
lessons.question: What does “sacrament of salvation” mean?
lessons.activity: “Read Lumen Gentium 1” (35 min). Students read the opening paragraph of Lumen Gentium and annotate: “sacrament,” “sign,” “instrument,” “union with God,” “unity of the whole human race.” Then write a paragraph explaining in plain words what it means that the Church is a sacrament, giving one example. Read Ephesians 5:25–32.
teach: The Church is the “universal sacrament of salvation” (CCC 774–776). She is the sign that points to Christ and the instrument through which he works.
“Mystery” (mysterion) in Ephesians means God’s hidden plan revealed in Christ (CCC 770–773). The Church is also the “bride” for whom Christ gave himself.
She originates in the Trinity: People of God of the Father, Body of Christ the Son, Temple of the Spirit (CCC 781–810).
This reading avoids two errors: the Church as a purely human institution, or as invisibly pure with no human structure.
talk: How is the Church a sacrament?
What is the difference between sign and instrument?
What does this say about her failings?
quiz: Calling the Church a “sacrament” (Lumen Gentium 1) means she is…|One of the seven sacraments|A sign and instrument of union with God and of the unity of mankind|A club|A building|1|CCC 775.
“Mystery” in Ephesians means…|A secret society|God’s hidden plan, now revealed in Christ (CCC 772)|A puzzle|A rumor|1|CCC 772.

Why is it misleading to treat the Church as only a human organization?|She has no laws|She has no members|She is also the Body of Christ, animated by the Spirit (CCC 779–780)|She has no history|2|CCC 779–780.
lessons.life: Read Lumen Gentium 1–8.
lessons.saint: Francis de Sales: a bishop who held that holiness belongs in every walk of life.
misc: “Sacrament” means the Church has the same status as Baptism.
lessons.mem: “The church is, in Christ, a kind of sacrament — a sign and instrument of communion with God and of unity among all men.” (Lumen Gentium 1)
lessons.hook: Show a wedding ring. “What does it do? It points to love and also helps create it.” A sacrament does the same thing, and the Church is the sacrament of Christ.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain in their own words why the Church is called a sacrament.

script.open: Say, “Think of a wedding ring. It’s a piece of metal. What else is it? How can a physical object be more than it appears?” Take answers. “That is the idea of a sacrament.”
teach: Say: “The Church is a mystery. In Catholic usage, mystery doesn’t mean a puzzle to solve but a reality with a divine depth that we can enter but never exhaust. Vatican II’s Lumen Gentium begins: ‘The Church, in Christ, is in the nature of a sacrament, a sign and instrument of communion with God and of the unity of the entire human race.’ A sacrament is a visible sign of an invisible grace. Christ himself is the original sacrament: the visible face of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15). The Church is the sacrament of Christ: she is his body and the sign through which he acts. The seven sacraments are the Church’s acts.”

Say: “The Church is one complex reality made of a human element and a divine element (LG 8). She has a visible structure: a Pope, bishops, parishes, buildings, laws. She is also a spiritual communion, the Body of Christ, a temple of the Spirit. These are not two churches; they are two aspects of one reality, like Jesus, who is one person with a human and divine nature. Gaudium et Spes calls her ‘a society of the faithful, and a mystical body.’ This is why scandals in the visible Church do not destroy her holiness: her holiness comes from Christ.”

Say: “What follows? The Church is not a club or an NGO. She cannot be evaluated only by sociology or efficiency. Nor can we dismiss the visible structure as unimportant. The Church is where we meet Christ in the sacraments, Scripture and community. The Church is both ‘holy and always in need of purification’ (LG 8), always in need of reform. She is a sinful people with a holy Lord. Francis de Sales loved the Church’s sacraments and knew people’s weaknesses. The Church is also a communion: the Greek koinonia means sharing in the life of the Trinity and in the life of each other.”
ask: What is a sacrament? (A visible sign of invisible grace.)
In what sense is the Church a sacrament? (A sign and instrument of union with God and of human unity.)
How can the Church be holy and need reform? (Her holiness is Christ’s; her members are sinners.)
practice: Draw two columns: “Visible” and “Invisible” aspects of the Church.
Fill in with at least five items each (Pope and bishops, buildings / grace, the Holy Spirit, communion of saints).
Draw arrows connecting pairs.
Write a paragraph: “Why the Church is not just a human organization.”
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make your Church a sign of your love.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look for the invisible in a visible sign at Mass.”

tryit: Define “sacrament” and “mystery.”
Give one example of each in the Church.
Explain how the Church is both visible and spiritual.
lessons.saintStory:
Francis de Sales was born in 1567 in Savoy, in the Alps. He studied law in Padua and was expected to have a brilliant career, but he chose to be a priest. In 1594 he volunteered for a dangerous mission to the Chablais, a region around Lake Geneva that had become Calvinist. People shut their doors on him. He trudged through snow, once sleeping in a tree to escape wolves. When nobody would listen, he wrote short pamphlets explaining the Catholic faith and slipped them under doors. Slowly, thousands returned to the Catholic Church.
He was made bishop of Geneva in 1602 and lived in Annecy. He was gentle, patient and cheerful: “A spoonful of honey attracts more flies than a barrel of vinegar.” In his book Introduction to the Devout Life, he taught that holiness is not just for monks, but for soldiers, workers and mothers. With Jane de Chantal, he started the Visitation sisters.
He died in 1622 and is the patron of writers. He is a Doctor of the Church.

lessons.title: People of God, Body of Christ, Temple of the Spirit
lessons.idea: Three biblical images describe the Church. She is the People of God (a priestly, prophetic, royal people), the Body of Christ (head and members, nourished by the Eucharist) and the Temple of the Holy Spirit (the Spirit as her soul).
lessons.question: Which image is most helpful?
lessons.activity: “Illustrate the three images” (35 min). Groups make an infographic for one image with: Scripture (1 Peter 2:9–10; 1 Corinthians 12:12–27; 1 Corinthians 3:16–17), meaning, consequences for how we live, and a modern example (parish, Eucharist, Spirit). Present and combine into a class booklet.
teach: People of God (CCC 781–786): chosen, redeemed, priestly, prophetic, kingly; the law is love. Body of Christ (CCC 787–795): Christ is head; Baptism and the Eucharist make us one body. Temple of the Spirit (CCC 797–801): the Spirit gives life, unity and charisms.
Together these correct each other: People of God stresses history and pilgrimage; Body, intimacy and unity; Temple, holiness.
Pope Pius XII’s Mystici Corporis (1943) is a classic text on the Body. Vatican II gave priority to People of God.
Ask students which image speaks to them now.
quiz: Which image stresses that Christ is the head and we are members?|People of God|Body of Christ (CCC 787–795)|Vineyard|Temple|1|1 Corinthians 12:12–27.
The “People of God” image emphasizes…|Hierarchy only|The past|The building|A pilgrim people chosen, redeemed and sharing in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and royal mission (CCC 781–786)|3|CCC 781–786.
The Spirit is called the “soul” of the Church because…|He replaces Christ|He is only a symbol|He is absent|He gives life, unity and gifts to the Body (CCC 797–798)|3|CCC 797–798.
lessons.life: Illustrate three images.
lessons.saint: Ananias of Damascus: a disciple who greeted his enemy as “Brother Saul.”
misc: “People of God means the Church is a democracy.”
“The Body of Christ is only a metaphor.”
lessons.mem: “Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.” (1 Corinthians 12:27)
lessons.hook: Show three objects: a team jersey, a body model, a temple model. “Each says something different about belonging.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain each image and what it implies for parish life.

script.open: Ask, “If you could describe your family in one image, what would you pick: a tree, a team, a house, a body? Why?” Take answers. “The Bible does the same with the Church.”
teach: Say: “The Church is the People of God. God called Abraham and Israel as a people. In Christ, he calls all nations. 1 Peter 2:9-10: ‘You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people… Once you were no people but now you are God’s people.’ The People of God have Christ as head, the Holy Spirit in their hearts, the law of love, and the Kingdom as their goal. Members are all baptized. The people share in Christ’s roles as priest, prophet and king.”

Say: “The Body of Christ. Paul uses this image in 1 Corinthians 12 and Romans 12. ‘For just as the body is one and has many members… so it is with Christ.’ We are many members with different gifts but one body. The head is Christ (Ephesians 1:22-23; Colossians 1:18). When one member suffers, all suffer; and Christ identifies with the body: ‘Why do you persecute me?’ The Eucharist makes the Church: we become what we receive (Augustine). The Church’s unity is not uniformity; it requires every member.”

Say: “The Temple of the Spirit. 1 Corinthians 3:16: ‘Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?’ The Spirit is the soul of the Body, giving life, unity, gifts and holiness. The Spirit gives each member charisms for the good of all. Other images: the Bride of Christ (Ephesians 5), the Flock, the Vine, the Field, the Building, the Family of God. Each shows an aspect. Together they say that the Church is a communion, not just an organization. Our response: we belong to the body, we use our gifts, we care for the weaker members, and we honor the Spirit in each person.”
ask: Name three images of the Church. (People of God, Body of Christ, Temple of the Spirit.)
Who is the head of the Body? (Christ.)
What does the Spirit give members? (Life, unity, charisms.)
practice: Choose three images and draw them.
Under each, write a Scripture verse and a one-sentence meaning.
Write what each image asks of a member: belonging, gifts, care.
Share your drawing with a partner and discuss which image speaks to you most.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make us one body.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look for the gifts you can bring to your parish.”

tryit: Match the biblical images with their meaning.
Draw one.
Say what each asks of members.
lessons.saintStory:
Ananias lived in Damascus, and was one of the disciples. The Lord spoke to him in a vision: “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul.” Ananias was horrified. “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem; and here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call upon your name.” The Lord said, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine.”
Ananias went, laid his hands on Saul, and said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Immediately something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and he was baptized.
Paul’s first experience of the Church was Ananias’s greeting, “Brother.” The Lord had said on the road: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” To strike the Church is to strike Christ.

lessons.title: One and holy
lessons.idea: The Church is one — in faith, sacraments and apostolic governance — and holy because Christ and the Spirit make her so. Divisions among Christians wound unity, and the Church works and prays for reunion.
lessons.question: Why is unity hard?
lessons.activity: “Discuss ecumenism” (35 min). A structured discussion: What unites Christians (Baptism, Scripture, the Creed)? What divides us (authority, sacraments, ministry)? What can we do (pray, study, serve together)? Review the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. Each student proposes a concrete step.
teach: The Church’s unity rests on one faith, shared sacramental life and apostolic succession (CCC 813–816). Unity is not uniformity: many rites and cultures coexist (CCC 814).
Holiness: the Church is holy because she is Christ’s Body, her means (Word and sacraments) are holy and the saints show her fruit; yet her members are sinners (CCC 823–829).

The Catholic Church works for Christian unity through prayer, dialogue and cooperation (CCC 820–822; Unitatis Redintegratio). The Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant communities differ in different degrees.
Name false irenicism: unity does not come by ignoring differences.
talk: How is the Church one yet divided?
How is she holy yet sinful?
quiz: Unity of the Church rests on…|One Lord, one faith, one Baptism, with the Pope and bishops as visible principle (CCC 813–815)|One nation|One language|Common custom|0|CCC 813–816.

Holiness of the Church means…|Christ and the Spirit sanctify her through the sacraments, and saints show it, though members are sinners (CCC 823–829)|Perfect conduct|Only clergy are holy|No member sins|0|CCC 823–829.
Ecumenism, for Catholics, seeks…|Absorbing others|Silence about differences|Christian unity in truth, through prayer, dialogue and service (CCC 820–822)|Merging all churches|2|CCC 820–822.
lessons.life: Pray daily for Christian unity.
lessons.saint: Frances Cabrini: a small, frail Italian sister who built hospitals and schools for immigrants.
lessons.mem: “That they may all be one… so that the world may believe that you have sent me.” (John 17:21)
lessons.hook: Read John 17:20–23, Jesus’ prayer for unity. Ask: “Why does he link our unity with the world’s belief?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain unity and holiness and propose one ecumenical action.

script.open: Show the Nicene Creed line “one, holy, catholic and apostolic.” Ask, “Looking at the Church honestly, is she one? Is she holy? What would you point to?” Take honest answers.
teach: Say: “The first mark is that the Church is one. Her unity comes from the Trinity: one Lord, one faith, one Baptism (Ephesians 4:5). The Church is one in her faith, her worship (the sacraments) and her government (apostolic succession, with the Pope as the visible center). But Christians are divided. The Catechism admits that ‘from the beginning, this one Church has been marked by a great variety’ (CCC 814), and that there have been wounds to unity: heresies, schisms. The Orthodox and Protestants have separated from full communion. Vatican II recognizes that ‘many elements of sanctification and of truth’ are found outside the visible boundaries of the Catholic Church. The Church works for ecumenism.”

Say: “The second mark is that the Church is holy. Not because every member is, but because her source is the holy God, her means are holy (the Word and sacraments), and she is the place where the holiness of the saints blossoms. Vatican II taught the universal call to holiness: ‘All the faithful, whatever their condition or state, are called by the Lord… to that perfection of sanctity by which the Father himself is perfect.’ (LG 11) The Church is ‘at once holy and always in need of purification.’ Holiness is shown in the saints. Mother Cabrini, an immigrant sister; Gianna Molla, a mother and doctor; Pier Giorgio Frassati, a student; Josemaría Escrivá, a priest. The Church’s holiness is visible in her works: hospitals, schools, charity.”

Say: “How do we hold unity and diversity together? Unity is not uniformity. The Church includes different rites, spiritualities and cultures. But unity requires communion: the same faith, sacraments and the bond with the bishops and the Pope. Holiness requires conversion: the Church kneels and confesses her sins in the liturgy: ‘I confess to almighty God and to you, my brothers and sisters.’ In 2000, John Paul II led the Church in a ‘purification of memory.’ The Church’s mission is to be a sign: ‘By this all men will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.’ (John 13:35)”
ask: Where does the Church’s unity come from? (The Trinity.)
What makes the Church holy? (Her holy source, means and the saints she produces.)
What did Vatican II say about holiness? (All are called to it.)
practice: Make two lists: signs of unity and signs of division in the Church today.
Make two more: signs of holiness and of sin.
Identify five saints from different states of life: a student, a mother, a worker, a priest, an immigrant.
Write a paragraph on how to respond when the Church disappoints you.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make us one, as you and the Father are one.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for the unity of Christians.”

tryit: Explain how the Church is one and yet divided.
List signs of holiness in the Church.
Name saints of different states of life.
lessons.saintStory:
Frances Cabrini was born in 1850 in Lombardy, Italy, the youngest of thirteen children. She was frail, and afraid of water after almost drowning. She wanted to be a missionary in China. After several rejections, she founded the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart in 1880.
She asked Pope Leo XIII to send her to China, but he said, “Not to the East, but to the West.” In 1889, she crossed the Atlantic to New York, where Italian immigrants were poor and often neglected. She started schools, orphanages and hospitals, from New York to Chicago, New Orleans, Seattle and Latin America. Though afraid of water, she crossed the ocean more than thirty times.
She became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 1909, and died in Chicago in 1917. In 1946 she became the first American citizen to be canonized. Her life was holiness in action.

lessons.title: Catholic and apostolic
lessons.idea: The Church is catholic: she has the fullness of faith and the means of salvation, and is sent to all peoples. She is apostolic: founded on the apostles, preserving their teaching, and led by their successors, the bishops.
lessons.question: What is apostolic succession?
lessons.activity: “Trace a bishop’s lineage” (35 min). Using apostolic succession charts, students trace their own bishop’s line of ordination back through earlier bishops (many dioceses publish this). Mark the link to the apostles. Discuss why apostolic succession matters (teaching, sacraments, unity).
teach: Catholic in two senses: the Church possesses the fullness of the means of salvation, and she is sent to the whole human race (CCC 830–831).
Apostolic: built on the foundation of the apostles (Ephesians 2:20), with their teaching kept by their successors (CCC 857–860). Bishops hand on their office by laying on of hands (CCC 861–862).
Irenaeus (c. 180) lists the bishops of Rome as proof of apostolic faith. Succession guarantees continuity of teaching and sacraments.
Distinguish “universal” from “Roman”: the Church includes Latin and Eastern rites.
quiz: “Catholic” in the Creed means…|Roman|Western|Large|According to the whole: the fullness of faith and means of salvation, for all peoples (CCC 830–831)|3|CCC 830–831.
Apostolic succession guarantees…|That bishops are sinless|The continuity of apostolic teaching and sacraments through bishops’ ordination (CCC 861–862)|Good manners|Wealth|1|CCC 861–862.
Which source early shows the importance of lists of bishops?|Dante|Augustine|Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3|The Didache only|2|Irenaeus cites the succession in Rome.
lessons.life: Find your bishop’s line of succession on a diocesan page.
lessons.saint: Boniface: an English monk who cut down a sacred oak and carried the faith across Germany.
lessons.mem: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.” (Acts 1:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What does ‘catholic’ mean?” (universal). Read Acts 1:8 and trace from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain two senses of “catholic” and what apostolic succession ensures.

script.open: Show a map of Europe. Ask, “How many countries use the name ‘Catholic’ for their main church? What does ‘catholic’ mean? What does ‘apostolic’ mean?” Take guesses.
teach: Say: “‘Catholic’ comes from the Greek katholikos, meaning ‘according to the whole.’ Ignatius of Antioch first used it around AD 107. The Church is catholic in two senses. First, because she has the fullness of the means of salvation: the whole faith, all the sacraments, and the apostolic ministry. Christ is present in her. Second, because she is sent to all people, in every age and place. Pentecost showed it: each heard in his own language. The Church is not tied to one culture; she adapts, as Boniface did: she built on what was good in the local culture and converted what was not. Catholic means universal, not uniform.”

Say: “‘Apostolic’ has three senses (CCC 857). One: the Church was founded on the apostles; Ephesians 2:20 speaks of the household of God ‘built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone.’ Two: she keeps and hands on the apostles’ teaching, the ‘deposit of faith.’ Three: she continues to be taught, sanctified and guided by the apostles’ successors, the college of bishops, assisted by the priests, together with the Pope, Peter’s successor. This is apostolic succession, going back by laying on of hands to the apostles. The word also means ‘sent’: the Church is apostolic because she is missionary.”

Say: “Why does it matter? Anyone can start a church and call it ‘Christian.’ Apostolic succession, the Church believes, ensures that she teaches what the apostles taught, that the sacraments are valid, and that she is united. The Orthodox Churches also have valid apostolic succession; Catholic teaching sees them as true Churches though not in full communion with the Pope. Most Protestant communities do not claim this succession. The Catholic Church holds that the Church of Christ ‘subsists in’ the Catholic Church (LG 8) with the fullness of means, while recognizing that ‘many elements of sanctification and of truth’ are found outside. The Pope serves as the guarantor of unity.”
ask: What does catholic mean? (According to the whole; the fullness of faith for all peoples.)
What are three senses of apostolic? (Founded on the apostles, keeping their teaching, guided by their successors.)
What does the Pope guarantee? (Unity and fidelity.)
practice: Draw a chain of apostolic succession from Jesus to the apostles to your local bishop.
Ask: How could you find your bishop’s lineage? (Many dioceses list it.)
List three ways the Church is catholic in your parish (languages, cultures, ages).
Write a short answer to a friend who says, ‘Any church can claim to be Christ’s.’
script.close: Pray: “Lord, keep us faithful to the faith of the apostles.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look up the line of your bishop’s ordination.”

tryit: Define each term: catholic, apostolic.
Test them against a claim to be the Church.
Explain the Pope’s role in each.
lessons.saintStory:
Boniface was born around 675 in Wessex, England, and named Wynfrith. He became a Benedictine monk and a teacher. He felt called to missionary work among the Germanic peoples on the Continent. After a first attempt failed, he traveled to Rome, and in 719, Pope Gregory II sent him to Germany with a new name, Boniface, and a mission.
In about 723, at Geismar, he confronted the pagan cult of the god Donar (Thor) by taking an axe to a huge oak sacred to him. People waited for the god to strike him dead. When nothing happened, many were converted. He built a chapel with the wood. He founded monasteries and brought English nuns and monks to help. Boniface was made archbishop and always kept loyalty to the Pope.
In 754, in his late seventies, he went back to preach among the Frisians. On June 5, at Dokkum, a band of raiders attacked his party. According to tradition, he held up a book of the Gospels to protect himself and was killed. He is the “Apostle of Germany.”

lessons.title: Hierarchy and laity
lessons.idea: The Church has a hierarchical structure — Pope, bishops, priests, deacons — and a vast laity, along with consecrated life. All have different roles but share equal dignity as baptized members and the call to holiness.
lessons.question: What is the role of the laity?
lessons.activity: “Interview people in ministry” (40 min). Students prepare questions and interview (in person or by recorded interview) a priest, deacon, religious sister or brother, a lay catechist or parish worker. Ask: how they were called, what their day looks like, joys and challenges. Present insights.
teach: The hierarchy exists to serve: the Pope is the visible head of the college of bishops (CCC 880–882); bishops teach, sanctify and govern (CCC 888–896); priests are co-workers with the bishop (CCC 1562–1568); deacons serve (CCC 1569–1571).
The laity share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly office and have a special mission to sanctify the world from within (CCC 897–913).
Consecrated life — the evangelical counsels lived in community or alone — is a gift to the Church (CCC 914–933).
Equal dignity, different functions (CCC 872). Clericalism and passivity are both distortions.
talk: What is the role of the laity?
quiz: The laity’s special mission is…|To seek the Kingdom by ordering temporal affairs according to God’s will (CCC 898)|Ceremonial duties|To replace clergy|To avoid public life|0|CCC 898.
Priests are, in relation to the bishop,…|Rivals|Equals|His servants only|His co-workers, sharing in his ministry (CCC 1562–1568)|3|CCC 1562–1568.
Consecrated life is…|A higher class of Christians|Dangerous|Required|A gift to the Church and a sign of the Kingdom (CCC 916, 933)|3|CCC 916.
lessons.life: Interview a layperson in ministry.
lessons.saint: Josemaría Escrivá: a priest who taught that ordinary work can be holy.
misc: “Priests and nuns are holier by nature.”
lessons.mem: “And he gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, some as pastors and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry.” (Ephesians 4:11–12)
lessons.hook: Read Ephesians 4:11–16. Ask: “Why does Paul say ‘to equip the saints’? Who does the work of ministry?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the roles of hierarchy, laity and consecrated life.

script.open: Ask, “If I said ‘Church leader,’ whom would you picture? Now picture a Church member who is a nurse, an engineer or a student. Is one more ‘in the Church’ than the other?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Church is structured. Vatican II describes the People of God as having ordained ministers and lay faithful, all equal in dignity by Baptism but with different roles. The hierarchy is composed of bishops, priests and deacons. The Pope is the bishop of Rome and the successor of Peter, with supreme authority in the Church. Bishops are successors of the apostles, who lead dioceses and together form the College of Bishops, with the Pope as head. Priests assist the bishop, preaching, celebrating the sacraments, and leading parishes. Deacons serve in word, liturgy and charity. The word ‘hierarchy’ means ‘sacred rule,’ but Jesus said the leader must be a servant (Mark 10:42-45).”

Say: “The laity are all the baptized who are not ordained or in the consecrated state. By Baptism, they share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and royal mission. Their special field is the world: family, work, culture, politics, economics, the media. ‘The laity, by their very vocation, seek the kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs and directing them according to the plan of God.’ (LG 31) The laity also have roles within the Church: readers, catechists, parish councils, Eucharistic ministers, teachers, theologians, pastoral associates. Lay people are about 99.9 percent of the Church. The mission of the Church to the world is carried mostly by the laity.”

Say: “The consecrated life includes religious (monks, nuns, friars, sisters) who profess vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, as well as consecrated virgins, hermits and members of secular institutes. They aren’t a third class between clergy and laity but a sign of the Kingdom. Different roles do not mean different value. The Church is communion: the hierarchy serves the people, and the people support the hierarchy. A common error is clericalism, thinking that only the clergy ‘are the Church.’ Pope Francis has repeatedly warned against it. The opposite error would be to disregard the authority Christ gave to the apostles. St. Josemaría’s message: your work is a path to holiness.”
ask: Name the three degrees of Holy Orders. (Bishops, priests, deacons.)
What is the laity’s special field? (The world: family, work, culture.)
What is clericalism? (Treating the clergy as the only real Church.)
practice: Draw a chart showing the roles in the Church: Pope, bishops, priests, deacons, religious, laity.
For each, write one task and one Scripture reference.
Under the laity, write five ordinary jobs and how each could be a path to holiness.
Write a one-sentence offering of your own work or studies.
script.close: Pray the Morning Offering. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Offer your next piece of homework to God as prayer.”

tryit: Fill in who does what in the Church.
Name the laity’s role in the world.
Write one way to sanctify your work.
lessons.saintStory:
Josemaría Escrivá was born in 1902 in Barbastro, Spain. After his father’s business failed and the family fell into poverty, he decided to become a priest, and was ordained in 1925. On October 2, 1928, during a retreat, he said he “saw” what God wanted: a way for ordinary people to pursue holiness in their daily work. He founded Opus Dei, “Work of God.”
He taught that all baptized people are called to holiness, and that work, family life and friendships can all be paths to God. “There is something holy, something divine, hidden in the most ordinary situations, and it is up to each one of you to discover it.” The members were lay people, professionals, students and workers who stayed in their jobs.
The Spanish Civil War forced him into hiding. Opus Dei grew to tens of thousands of members in many countries. He died in 1975 and was canonized in 2002. Vatican II, in teaching the universal call to holiness, echoed his message.

units.title: Church history I: the early Church

lessons.title: Pentecost to Constantine
lessons.idea: From Pentecost to Constantine the Church grew through persecution. Martyrs such as Stephen, Ignatius, Polycarp, Perpetua and Felicity bore witness, and by 313 Christians were free to worship. “The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church.”
lessons.question: Why did persecution fail?
lessons.activity: “Read martyr acts” (35 min). Groups read short excerpts from the Martyrdom of Polycarp, the Letter to the Romans by Ignatius and the Passion of Perpetua. Each group answers: What were they accused of? What did they say? What kept them going? What does this say about faith?
teach: The Church spread across the Roman Empire amid sporadic and later systematic persecution (Nero, Decius, Diocletian). Christians refused to offer incense to the emperor (CCC 2473–2474).
The early Church’s distinguishing features: Eucharist on Sunday, care for the poor, rejection of abortion and infanticide, fidelity in marriage (Didache, Justin Martyr).
In 313 Constantine and Licinius issued the Edict of Milan, granting freedom to Christians. Theodosius made Christianity the empire’s religion in 380.
Mention modern martyrs and the witness of persecuted Christians today.
quiz: Why did Christians refuse to burn incense to the emperor?|They disliked the smell|It would be an act of worship due to God alone|It was a food rule|They were tax resisters|1|CCC 2473.
The Edict of Milan (313) did what?|Granted freedom of worship to Christians|Called Nicaea|Made Christianity the only religion|Banned paganism|0|Constantine and Licinius.
Early Christian practices that stood out in the Roman world included…|Gladiator games|Care for the poor and rejection of abortion and infanticide (Didache)|Imperial cult|Child exposure|1|Didache 2.
lessons.life: Read the Martyrdom of Polycarp.
lessons.saint: Cyprian of Carthage: a bishop who held the Church together through persecution and plague.
lessons.mem: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.” (Revelation 2:10)
lessons.hook: Read Revelation 2:10: “Be faithful unto death.” Ask: “What would make someone say that and mean it?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe how the early Church grew and the witness of two martyrs.

script.open: Ask, “Under pressure, what would make you hide your faith? Be honest: social media, friends, jobs, fear?” Let students think. “The early Church faced this at a deadly scale.”
teach: Say: “From Pentecost to Constantine is almost 300 years. The early Church began in Jerusalem, a Jewish community, and spread through the Roman Empire along roads and sea lanes. Paul’s missionary journeys took the Gospel to Asia Minor and Greece, and then to Rome. By AD 100, there were Christians in most major cities. By 300, perhaps 5 to 10 percent of the empire. The Church grew by personal witness: the way Christians lived, cared for the poor and sick, treated women, refused to abandon infants (as pagans did), and faced death.”

Say: “Persecution was sporadic and local until the third century. Nero blamed Christians for the fire in Rome in AD 64. Domitian’s time. Trajan told Pliny: Christians must not be sought out, but punished if denounced. Decius in 250 began the first empire-wide persecution. Valerian in 257. And Diocletian’s Great Persecution, 303-311, was the worst: churches burned, Scriptures destroyed, clergy arrested. In response, the Church developed her organization. Bishops led dioceses, synods met, a canon of Scripture took shape, and the Eucharistic liturgy was settled. The writers called Apologists defended Christians. Tertullian: ‘The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church.’”

Say: “In 313, Constantine and Licinius issued the Edict of Milan. Constantine favored the Church, built basilicas, and called the Council of Nicaea in 325. Theodosius made Christianity the empire’s religion in 380. The change brought opportunity and danger: the Church was no longer persecuted, but could be politically entangled, and nominal membership grew. Monasticism arose partly as a protest: those who wanted a radical life went to the desert. A lesson from Cyprian: in crisis, the Church must hold truth and mercy together, neither compromising the faith nor driving away the weak. The early Church shows what a faithful minority can do.”
ask: Name a persecution. (Nero, Decius, Diocletian.)
What did Cyprian decide about the lapsed? (Penance, then restoration.)
What did Constantine’s Edict of Milan do? (Granted freedom of worship.)
practice: Make a timeline from AD 30 to 380 with ten events: Pentecost, Paul’s journeys, Nero, destruction of Jerusalem (70), Ignatius (107), Decius (250), Diocletian (303), Milan (313), Nicaea (325), Theodosius (380).
Mark persecutions in red and growth in green.
Write what the Church learned from the lapsed.
Compare with what pressures Christians face today.
script.close: Pray for persecuted Christians today. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for the courage to stand for your faith.”

tryit: Make a timeline of the persecutions.
Mark how the Church responded to the lapsed.
Write what the Church learned.
lessons.saintStory:
Cyprian was a wealthy lawyer and teacher of rhetoric in Carthage, North Africa. He became a Christian around 246, gave away much of his wealth, and within two years was made bishop of Carthage. In 250, Emperor Decius ordered all citizens to sacrifice to the gods. Many Christians gave in. Cyprian went into hiding and directed his flock by letters, a decision for which he was criticized.
After the persecution, he faced a crisis: what to do with the lapsed, Christians who had sacrificed or bought certificates saying they had? Some confessors wanted instant forgiveness; some wanted to ban them forever. Cyprian chose a middle way: they must do penance and then could be restored. In 252, a plague hit Carthage. Pagans abandoned the sick. Cyprian urged Christians to care for everyone, including their enemies.
He wrote On the Unity of the Church: “He cannot have God for his Father who has not the Church for his mother.” In 258, in a new persecution, he refused to sacrifice and was beheaded.

lessons.title: The Councils and the Creeds
lessons.idea: The first ecumenical councils defined who Christ and the Holy Spirit are: Nicaea (325) taught that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, Constantinople I (381) the divinity of the Spirit, Ephesus (431) that Mary is Theotokos, Chalcedon (451) the two natures of Christ.
lessons.question: What did Nicaea decide and why?
lessons.activity: “Study Arianism” (35 min). Students compare Arius’ claim (“there was when he was not”) and Athanasius’ reply with texts from John 1, John 10:30, Colossians 1:15–20. Then trace how the Nicene Creed responded. Discuss: why does it matter if Christ is God for our salvation?
teach: Arianism taught that the Son was the first and greatest creature, not eternal and not of the same being as the Father. Nicaea defined him “consubstantial” (homoousios) with the Father (CCC 242, 465).
Constantinople I affirmed the divinity of the Holy Spirit and completed the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed. Ephesus declared Mary Theotokos; Chalcedon taught one Person in two natures (CCC 466–469).
Athanasius: only God can save, so the Savior must be God (On the Incarnation). Doctrinal clarity is a service to love.
The councils’ authority comes from their reception by the Church and confirmation by the Pope.
quiz: Arius taught that the Son…|Is the Spirit|Was a prophet only|Is a creature, first and greatest|Is equal to the Father|2|CCC 465 context.
Nicaea’s key word “homoousios” means…|A mystery|Of similar substance|Of the same substance with the Father|Of different substance|2|CCC 242.
Which council taught one Person in two natures?|Jerusalem|Chalcedon|Trent|Vatican I|1|CCC 467.
lessons.life: Compare the Nicene Creed with the Apostles’ Creed.
lessons.saint: Hilary of Poitiers: a bishop who was exiled for defending the Trinity.
misc: “Councils voted on whether Jesus was God.”
lessons.mem: “We believe in one Lord, Jesus Christ… God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.” (Nicene Creed)
lessons.hook: Read John 1:1–3. Ask: “Was the Word created, or was he always?” Introduce Arius’ answer and why it mattered.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Arianism, the Nicene response and why it matters for salvation.

script.open: Write the first line of the Nicene Creed on the board. Ask, “Why do we say the Creed every Sunday? Who wrote it? Why so many words?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The first Christian creeds were short baptismal professions: ‘Jesus is Lord’ (Romans 10:9), then the questions in three parts: ‘Do you believe in God the Father… in Jesus Christ… in the Holy Spirit?’ That became the Apostles’ Creed, an old Roman baptismal creed. As heresies arose, the Church needed more precise language. The ecumenical councils produced the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed, which we pray at Mass. Councils are gatherings of bishops from around the world, called to settle questions of faith. The Church recognizes 21 ecumenical councils, from Nicaea I (325) to Vatican II (1962-65).”

Say: “The first four councils defined the Trinity and Christ. Nicaea I (325): the Son is ‘consubstantial’ (homoousios) with the Father, against Arius. Constantinople I (381): the Holy Spirit is God, ‘who with the Father and the Son is adored and glorified,’ against those who denied the Spirit’s divinity. Ephesus (431): Mary is Theotokos, against Nestorius; Jesus is one Person. Chalcedon (451): Jesus has two natures, divine and human, in one Person, against Monophysitism. Later, Constantinople II (553) and III (680-81) completed the picture, with two wills in Christ. Nicaea II (787) approved the veneration of icons, against iconoclasm.”

Say: “Why was this not just hair-splitting? Each word protects the Gospel. If the Son is not truly God, then Jesus cannot save us. If he’s not truly man, he cannot represent us. The word ‘homoousios’ was not in the Bible, but it expressed what the Bible says. Hilary and Athanasius saw that the whole of Christian life depends on it. The Creed is also a prayer, and the Church’s summary of the faith. It is not an opinion poll but a gift received. The ‘filioque’ clause (the Spirit proceeds from the Father ‘and the Son’) was added in the West and is still a difference with the Orthodox. Councils also settled calendar questions (Easter date) and church order.”
ask: What did Nicaea declare? (The Son is consubstantial with the Father.)
What did Chalcedon teach? (Christ has two natures in one Person.)
Why do councils matter? (They protect the faith.)
practice: Make a table of the first four councils: year, heresy, teaching, line in the Creed.
Underline the key word (homoousios, Theotokos, two natures).
Write each in simple English.
Pray the Creed slowly, noticing each line.
script.close: Pray the Nicene Creed aloud together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray the Creed at Mass, thinking of Hilary.”

tryit: Trace how the Creed grew.
Match each heresy with its council.
Explain each line of the Creed it defends.
lessons.saintStory:
Hilary was born around 310 in Gaul, to a pagan family. A scholar, he read the Scriptures in search of the truth about God, and was struck by John 1:1, “In the beginning was the Word.” He was baptized in his thirties, was married with a daughter, and around 350 was elected bishop of Poitiers.
Emperor Constantius II supported the Arians, and pressured the Western bishops to condemn Athanasius. Hilary refused. In 356 he was exiled to Phrygia, in Asia Minor, for about four years. There he studied Eastern theology and wrote On the Trinity, a major work defending the divinity of the Son. He also wrote commentaries on Matthew and the Psalms. He was allowed back, and returned to Gaul to work for peace.
He died in 367. He was called the “Athanasius of the West” and is a Doctor of the Church.

lessons.title: The Church Fathers
lessons.idea: The Fathers of the Church — Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine — handed on the apostolic faith, defended it against heresy, and wrote commentaries, sermons and treatises that still guide us.
lessons.question: What do the Fathers teach us?
lessons.activity: “Read a Father” (35 min). Students choose an excerpt from Ignatius (Smyrnaeans 6–7, on the Eucharist), Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.3, on succession) or Augustine (Confessions 8, his conversion). They summarize, note the context, and write one sentence on what it teaches about the faith.
teach: The Fathers are witnesses to Tradition (CCC 11, 78, 688, 2651). Criteria for a Father: antiquity, orthodoxy, holiness, Church approval.
Greek Fathers: Athanasius, the Cappadocians (Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa), John Chrysostom. Latin Fathers: Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory the Great.
Their method: read Scripture with the Church, defend the faith, form believers. Their agreement (consensus patrum) is significant.
Include women who shaped the age: Monica, Macrina, Paula.
quiz: A Father of the Church is characterized by…|Writing in Greek|Fame|Antiquity, orthodoxy, holiness and Church approval|Being a bishop|2|CCC 11, 78.
Which pair are Latin Fathers?|Chrysostom and Gregory of Nyssa|Origen and Ignatius|Ambrose and Augustine|Athanasius and Basil|2|Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory the Great.
The “consensus of the Fathers” matters because…|It is mathematically proven|Their agreement witnesses to the faith handed on (Dei Verbum 8)|They were perfect|They voted|1|Dei Verbum 8.
lessons.life: Read from Athanasius’s On the Incarnation.
lessons.saint: Isidore of Seville: a bishop who gathered the learning of the ancient world into one book.
misc: “The Fathers are only relevant to scholars.”
lessons.mem: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” (Acts 2:42)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Who was the first to put into words something you believe?” Introduce the Fathers as the Church’s early teachers.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three Fathers, one contribution each and why they matter.

script.open: Ask, “If you could ask a question of someone who lived in the year 200, who would you choose, and what would you ask?” Take answers. “The Fathers are those voices.”
teach: Say: “The Fathers of the Church are Christian writers of the first centuries whose teaching is a witness to the apostolic faith. Four marks: orthodoxy of doctrine, holiness of life, Church approval, and antiquity. Different groups: the Apostolic Fathers (Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp, the Didache); the Apologists (Justin, Tertullian); the Greek Fathers (Athanasius, Basil, the two Gregorys, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria); the Latin Fathers (Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory the Great, Isidore). Eastern Fathers wrote on the Trinity and spiritual life; Western Fathers on grace, the Church and law.”

Say: “What they gave. They interpreted the Scriptures, especially through the spiritual senses. They defended the faith against heresies. They developed theological language. They gave catechesis to converts and preached on the sacraments. They also modeled holiness. Their testimony to the liturgy is valuable. Justin describes the Mass in AD 155. The Didache (around AD 100) describes Baptism, fasting and the Eucharist. Ignatius and Irenaeus defend the Real Presence. Cyprian and Augustine write of the Church. Without the Fathers, we would not have the Creed or the canon.”

Say: “Weigh them carefully. The Fathers are not infallible individually; they sometimes disagreed or erred on secondary matters. Origen’s speculations were condemned; Augustine’s view of limbo was a theory. What matters is their moral unanimity on matters of faith (consensus patrum). Vatican II says their writings ‘testify to the living presence of this Tradition.’ (DV 8) Protestants also value the Fathers, though differ in interpretation. The Liturgy of the Hours includes readings from them each day. Reading the Fathers helps us see that the Catholic faith is ancient. Some good starting points: Augustine’s Confessions, Athanasius’s On the Incarnation, Chrysostom’s homilies, and Gregory’s Pastoral Rule.”
ask: Who are the Fathers? (Early writers whose teaching witnesses to the apostolic faith.)
Name a Greek Father and a Latin Father. (Athanasius; Augustine.)
What does the consensus of the Fathers show? (What the Church believed from the beginning.)
practice: Give each pair a short Father excerpt (Ignatius on the Eucharist, Justin on the Mass, Irenaeus on Mary, Augustine on grace).
Write: what question does this answer, and what does it show about early belief?
Rate how useful this is for a modern Catholic.
Share findings.
script.close: Pray a collect of the Father you read. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read a Father’s homily in the Office of Readings.”

tryit: Read a short excerpt from a Father.
Say what question it answers.
Rate its usefulness today.
lessons.saintStory:
Isidore was born around 560 in Spain, into a family of saints: his brothers Leander and Fulgentius and his sister Florentina were all honored as saints. After the Visigoths conquered Spain, Leander, the archbishop of Seville, raised Isidore, and when Leander died, Isidore succeeded him around 600. He served for over thirty years.
Isidore was concerned that with the collapse of the Roman Empire, ancient learning would be lost. He wrote the Etymologies, a twenty-book encyclopedia of everything: grammar, medicine, law, agriculture, the heavens, war, ships, animals, buildings, and the Church. He explained things by tracing the origin of words. It became the standard reference for the Middle Ages, copied in hundreds of manuscripts. He also presided at the Fourth Council of Toledo (633) which required every cathedral to set up a school.
He died in 636. He is a Doctor of the Church, and has been proposed as the patron of the internet.

units.title: Church history II: Middle Ages to modernity

lessons.title: Monasticism and mission
lessons.idea: Monasticism began in the desert with Anthony and Pachomius, and Benedict gave it a lasting form. Monks and missionaries such as Columban, Boniface and Cyril and Methodius evangelized Europe, copied manuscripts and built culture.
lessons.question: How did monasteries shape Europe?
lessons.activity: “Present on Benedict or Boniface” (40 min). Students prepare a five-minute presentation on a monk or missionary: context, work, quote, legacy. Include maps. Class feedback: what does this witness teach about faith and culture?
teach: Monasticism (CCC 918–927): from the hermits of Egypt (Anthony c. 270) to communities (Pachomius), to the Benedictine Rule (c. 530): prayer, work, study, hospitality, stability.

Missionary monks: Patrick (Ireland), Columba and Columban (Scotland and the Continent), Augustine of Canterbury (England), Boniface (Germany), Cyril and Methodius (Slavic lands). They translated Scripture and the liturgy.
Monasteries preserved classical learning, developed agriculture, medicine and music, and cared for travelers.
Avoid “Dark Ages” myths; acknowledge the real collapse of Roman order.
talk: What is a rule of life?
quiz: Benedict’s Rule is known for…|Violence|A balanced life of prayer, work, study and hospitality|Isolation|Wealth|1|CCC 918–927.
Which missionary evangelized Germany?|Augustine of Canterbury|Patrick|Columba|Boniface|3|Boniface, 8th century.
Monasteries preserved learning by…|Copying manuscripts|Selling books|Burning books|Ignoring texts|0|Scriptoria.
lessons.life: Read a page of the Rule of Benedict.
lessons.saint: Patrick: a former slave who returned to convert his captors.
lessons.mem: “If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” (Matthew 19:21)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you take if you were going into the desert for the rest of your life?” Read Matthew 19:21.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how monks shaped Europe and name two missionaries.

script.open: Ask, “How would you feel about returning to a country where you had been enslaved, to help the people who enslaved you? What would make you do it?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “After Rome’s fall in 476, Europe was fragmented. Monasteries became the centers of civilization. Benedict’s Rule (around 530) shaped Western monasticism with ‘pray and work.’ Irish monasteries, following Patrick, became centers of learning and mission: Columba founded Iona (563), Columbanus went to the Continent and founded Luxeuil and Bobbio. Anglo-Saxon missionaries: Augustine of Canterbury (597), Aidan, Bede, Boniface in Germany. Cyril and Methodius to the Slavs. By about 1000, nearly all Europe was Christian. Monks copied manuscripts, preserving the Bible, the Fathers and classical works. They farmed, taught and welcomed travelers.”

Say: “The Church and the new rulers. Clovis, king of the Franks, was baptized around 496. Charlemagne was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day, 800. This produced a close relationship of Church and state, with benefits and problems. Bishops became feudal lords. Kings appointed bishops, known as lay investiture. Pope Gregory VII (1073-85) led a reform movement, insisting the Church be free from lay control and clergy be celibate. The conflict with Emperor Henry IV culminated in his penance at Canossa in 1077. The monastic reform movements, such as Cluny, the Cistercians and Carthusians, renewed the Church.”

Say: “The high Middle Ages, 1100-1300, were the Church’s great period of building and learning. The mendicant orders (Franciscans, Dominicans) preached in cities. Universities rose. Scholastic theology blossomed with Anselm, Abelard, Bonaventure and Aquinas. Gothic cathedrals rose. There were also darker features: the Crusades, the Inquisition, anti-Jewish violence, and corruption in some of the clergy and papacy. The popes moved to Avignon (1309-1377) and a Western Schism (1378-1417) produced rival popes. These abuses prepared the ground for the Reformation. A fair view is that the medieval Church was a mixture of holiness and corruption, but the faith sank deep roots in European culture.”
ask: Who evangelized Ireland? (Patrick.)
Who was crowned emperor in 800? (Charlemagne.)
What was the Western Schism? (A period when rival claimants to the papacy divided the Church.)
practice: On a map of Europe, mark key monasteries (Monte Cassino, Iona, Luxeuil, Cluny, Clairvaux), the baptism of Clovis, and Charlemagne’s coronation.
Draw arrows for the missions.
Write a list of what the monks preserved.
Compare the strengths and weaknesses of the Church in the Middle Ages.
script.close: Pray the Breastplate of Saint Patrick or: “Christ with me, Christ before me.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look up Patrick’s Confession.”

tryit: Trace the spread of the faith on a map.
Mark the monasteries.
Say what the monks preserved.
lessons.saintStory:
Patrick was born around 385 in Roman Britain, the son of a deacon and grandson of a priest. At sixteen, he was kidnapped by Irish raiders and taken to Ireland as a slave, where he tended sheep for six years. He had not taken faith seriously before, but alone on the hills, he began to pray, “a hundred times a day and almost as many at night.”
After six years, he heard a voice in a dream telling him that his ship was ready. He escaped, traveled two hundred miles to the coast and found passage to Britain. He later had a dream in which a man named Victoricus gave him a letter: “The Voice of the Irish.” In it, people from Ireland were calling, “Holy boy, come and walk among us again.”
He studied for the priesthood, was ordained a bishop and returned to Ireland around 432. He baptized thousands, and trained clergy and founded churches. He wrote the Confession, a humble account of his life. He is said to have used the shamrock to teach the Trinity. He died around 461.

lessons.title: Schisms and Reformation
lessons.idea: The Church suffered two great divisions: the Great Schism of 1054 between East and West, and the Protestant Reformation from 1517. Each had real causes, theological and political, and left wounds that the Church is working to heal.
lessons.question: What caused the divisions?
lessons.activity: “Compare beliefs” (40 min). Students build a three-column table: Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant. Rows: authority (Pope, patriarchs, Scripture alone), sacraments (seven, seven, two or three), Eucharist, Mary and saints, justification, Church structure. Mark the points of agreement. Discuss respectfully.
teach: The Eastern Orthodox share apostolic succession, sacraments and the early creeds with Catholics; the main differences are papal primacy and jurisdiction, the Filioque, and some doctrines (CCC 817–819, 838).

The Reformation began with Luther’s protest against indulgence abuses (1517) and expanded to disputes over authority, justification, sacraments and the Mass. Reformers (Luther, Zwingli, Calvin) and Henry VIII’s break with Rome (1534) produced Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican communities.
The Catholic Church sees in those communities genuine elements of sanctification and truth (CCC 819), and works toward unity. Today there are 40,000+ Protestant denominations of very different kinds.
Guard against caricature of either side. Include both blame and admission of fault (CCC 817).
talk: What do Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants share?
quiz: A main issue between East and West in 1054 was…|Mary|Baptism|The Creed’s existence|Papal primacy and jurisdiction, and the Filioque|3|CCC 838.
Luther’s Ninety-five Theses (1517) first challenged…|Abuses in the preaching and sale of indulgences|Scripture|The Mass|The papacy directly|0|Reformation context.

The Church’s present view of Protestant communities includes…|They have nothing|Real elements of sanctification and truth, with Baptism as bond (CCC 818–819)|They are the same|They are enemies|1|CCC 818–819.
lessons.life: Compare the beliefs of the three groups.
lessons.saint: John Fisher: the only bishop in England who refused to bow to Henry VIII.
misc: “Luther wanted to start a new church.”
lessons.mem: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree.” (1 Corinthians 1:10)
lessons.hook: Show a family tree with branches cut. Read John 17:21. Ask: “How do families break?” Misunderstanding, pride, hurt, real disagreements.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe one similarity and one difference among the three traditions.

script.open: Ask, “When something is badly broken in an institution you love, there are three responses: leave, tear it down, or reform it. Which is the right one, and when?” Take answers. “The sixteenth century faced exactly this.”
teach: Say: “Medieval schisms: the East-West Schism of 1054 split Rome from the Eastern Churches; the Western Schism of 1378-1417 had two and then three claimants to the papacy. In the late Middle Ages, the Church was weakened by corruption: bishops who held many offices and didn’t reside in their dioceses, poorly trained clergy, selling of indulgences, and fighting among popes and princes. Reformers like John Wycliffe in England and Jan Hus in Bohemia had called for change, and Hus was burned. There were saints, too: Catherine of Siena, Bernardino, Vincent Ferrer. The Renaissance popes spent lavishly on art and war. Gutenberg’s printing press (1450s) spread ideas quickly. Nationalism and kings wanting power also mattered.”

Say: “Luther’s protest in 1517 started a spiral. By 1521 he was excommunicated. In Switzerland, Zwingli and Calvin rejected much of Catholic worship and sacramental teaching. The Peace of Augsburg (1555) let each prince choose Lutheran or Catholic faith for his realm. In England, Henry VIII separated from Rome in 1534 for political and personal reasons, but doctrine changed under Edward VI and Elizabeth I. Wars of religion devastated Europe, such as the Thirty Years’ War (1618-48). The Reformers raised legitimate questions: Scripture, grace, abuses. But the Catholic Church holds that they went too far in rejecting the sacraments, the priesthood, the papacy and Tradition.”

Say: “Different views on the split. Protestants speak of the recovery of the Gospel. Catholics speak of a tragic rupture. Today many scholars see it as both. What happened afterward: the Catholic Reformation (Trent, Jesuits, saints) renewed the Church; Protestant churches multiplied. Today, about 2.3 billion Christians: 1.4 billion Catholic, about 1 billion Protestant and Anglican, 260 million Orthodox. The 500th anniversary in 2017 was marked by common prayer; Pope Francis traveled to Sweden to join Lutherans. We can acknowledge that both sides sinned. The Catechism: ‘The Church’s ecumenical task…’ requires repentance and prayer for unity.”
ask: What caused the Reformation? (Abuses, Luther’s questions, printing, politics.)
Who refused the Act of Supremacy among the bishops? (John Fisher.)
What was the Peace of Augsburg? (Each prince chose Lutheran or Catholic faith for his realm.)
practice: Make a table: Cause, Type (abuse, doctrine, politics), Catholic response.
Include at least eight items.
Draw a line to separate things the Church admitted were wrong from things she defended.
Write a paragraph beginning, “If I had lived in 1517, I would have…”
script.close: Pray for the unity of all Christians. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Learn the difference between Catholic and Lutheran beliefs.”

tryit: Sort the causes of the Reformation.
Mark which were abuses and which were doctrines.
Write what the Church lost and gained.
lessons.saintStory:
John Fisher was born in 1469 in Yorkshire. He became bishop of Rochester in 1504, a small poor diocese, which he served for over thirty years and refused to leave for richer ones. He was one of the most learned men in England, a patron of scholars like Erasmus, and a chancellor of Cambridge University. He lived simply and was devoted to his flock. He preached against Luther’s teaching, and also called for reform within the Church.
When Henry VIII sought to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Fisher defended the marriage in court, saying he would die for it. In 1534, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, making the king head of the Church of England. Fisher was the only bishop to refuse the oath. He was imprisoned in the Tower of London. In 1535, the pope made him a cardinal, and an angry Henry said he would send the head to Rome without a hat to put it on.
Fisher was beheaded on June 22, 1535, at sixty-six. Thomas More followed him two weeks later.

lessons.title: Vatican II and the modern era
lessons.idea: Vatican II (1962–1965) renewed the Church’s mission for the modern world. Its four constitutions — Lumen Gentium, Dei Verbum, Sacrosanctum Concilium and Gaudium et Spes — reflect on the Church, Revelation, liturgy and the world. Its call to holiness and to engage the world continues.
lessons.question: What changed and what stayed?
lessons.activity: “Summarize four constitutions” (40 min). Groups read an excerpt from each constitution and summarize: main idea, a key phrase, a practical fruit, a continuing debate. Create a one-page summary card for each and swap.
teach: John XXIII called the Council to “open the windows” and renew the Church’s presentation of unchanging faith (CCC 10–11). It issued 16 documents.

Lumen Gentium: the Church as People of God, universal call to holiness. Dei Verbum: Scripture and Tradition. Sacrosanctum Concilium: active participation, vernacular. Gaudium et Spes: engagement with modern world, dignity of the person.
Other major documents: Unitatis Redintegratio (ecumenism), Nostra Aetate (other religions), Dignitatis Humanae (religious liberty).
The Council must be read in continuity with Tradition (a “hermeneutic of reform,” Benedict XVI).
talk: What is the hermeneutic of continuity?
quiz: Which is one of Vatican II’s four constitutions?|Rerum Novarum|Humanae Vitae|Dei Verbum|Unam Sanctam|2|Lumen Gentium, Dei Verbum, Sacrosanctum Concilium, Gaudium et Spes.
Sacrosanctum Concilium promoted…|Full, conscious and active participation in the liturgy|Fewer sacraments|Secret rites|Latin only|0|CCC 1071.
Benedict XVI’s “hermeneutic of reform” reads Vatican II as…|Renewal in continuity with the Church’s tradition|Doctrinal change|Irrelevant|A break with tradition|0|Address, 2005.
lessons.life: Read the first paragraph of Gaudium et Spes.
lessons.saint: Paul VI: the pope who steered the Council to its end and wrote Evangelii Nuntiandi.
lessons.mem: “You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden.” (Matthew 5:14)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 5:13–16 (salt and light). Ask: “How does the Church be salt and light in the modern world?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to summarize the four constitutions and one fruit of the Council.

script.open: Ask, “If you were told that the Church had changed everything after 1965, how would you test it? What would you look at?” Take answers. “Let’s look at what actually changed and what stayed.”
teach: Say: “Vatican II (1962-65) was the 21st ecumenical council. It began under John XXIII and ended under Paul VI. It produced four constitutions, nine decrees and three declarations. The main documents. Lumen Gentium: the Church as mystery, People of God, the hierarchy, the laity, the call to holiness, Mary. Dei Verbum: Revelation, Scripture and Tradition; encouragement to read the Bible. Sacrosanctum Concilium: reform of the liturgy, with ‘full, conscious and active participation’; the vernacular. Gaudium et Spes: the Church in the modern world, human dignity, marriage, culture, economics and peace. Also Nostra Aetate (other religions, rejecting antisemitism), Unitatis Redintegratio (ecumenism), Dignitatis Humanae (religious freedom).”

Say: “What changed? The Mass in local languages, the priest facing the people (not required, but common), greater use of Scripture, lay readers and ministers, a new Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults, the permanent diaconate was restored, ecumenical dialogue began, lay apostolate was encouraged. What did not change: doctrine, the Creed, the sacraments, the priesthood, the papacy, moral teaching. Pope Benedict XVI said there are two ‘hermeneutics’ or ways of reading the Council: a ‘hermeneutic of discontinuity and rupture,’ which sees the Council as a break with the past, and a ‘hermeneutic of reform,’ in which the Church renews herself while remaining the same subject. He affirmed the latter.”

Say: “The post-conciliar period was turbulent. Many left the priesthood and religious life in the 1960s-70s. Mass attendance fell in the West. Some believed the Council changed too much; some thought it had not gone far enough. The Council’s call to holiness, the Bible, and mission is still being implemented. Pope John Paul II called the Council ‘the great grace of the twentieth century.’ The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992) was the council’s fruit. Today, a key question: what does it mean to be a Church in dialogue with the world, faithful to Christ, confident in the Gospel? Paul VI’s Evangelii Nuntiandi gave one answer: the Church exists to evangelize.”
ask: Who closed Vatican II? (Paul VI.)
Name two changes after Vatican II. (Vernacular Mass; greater lay participation; ecumenism.)
What does a ‘hermeneutic of reform’ mean? (The Church renews while remaining the same.)
practice: Make a table of the four constitutions: main idea, one change, one thing to learn more about.
Add Nostra Aetate and Dignitatis Humanae.
Look up one paragraph of Lumen Gentium or Gaudium et Spes online and summarize it.
Write what you think the Council still asks of the Church.
script.close: Pray the Prayer for the Council or the Veni Creator. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read the opening of Gaudium et Spes.”

tryit: Match each document of Vatican II with its message.
Mark a change at your parish.
Write what the Council still asks.
lessons.saintStory:
Giovanni Battista Montini was born in 1897 in northern Italy and became a Vatican official, then archbishop of Milan, where he reached out to workers. He was elected pope in 1963 after John XXIII died, and took the name Paul. He was a thoughtful man, shy, who had a heavy responsibility: to lead Vatican II to its conclusion. He did so in 1965.
He was the first pope to travel by plane, going to the Holy Land in 1964, where he embraced the Orthodox patriarch Athenagoras, and to the United Nations in 1965, where he cried “No more war!” In December 1965, he and Athenagoras lifted the mutual excommunications of 1054. He reformed the Mass, set up the Synod of Bishops and the internationalization of the Curia.
He was criticized from all sides. His 1968 encyclical Humanae Vitae was widely rejected. He wrote in 1975 Evangelii Nuntiandi, a call to evangelization. He died in 1978 and was canonized in 2018.

lessons.title: Evangelization
lessons.idea: Evangelization means bringing the Good News to every person and making disciples. It includes witness, proclamation, dialogue and charity. The Church does not exist for herself but to proclaim Christ.
lessons.question: How do we evangelize today?
lessons.activity: “Plan a school witness” (40 min). In groups, students design a respectful witness for their school: a service day, a prayer group, an invitation to Mass, an acts-of-kindness week. Define purpose, steps, risk and how to speak about faith in gentle ways.
teach: The Church is missionary by nature (CCC 849–856; Ad Gentes). The mission comes from the Father’s own sending of the Son and the Spirit.
Evangelii Nuntiandi (Paul VI, 1975) says witness comes first, then proclamation. John Paul II called for a “new evangelization.” Pope Francis (Evangelii Gaudium) invites a joyful, missionary Church.
Dialogue is part of evangelization, but not a replacement for proclamation (Dialogue and Proclamation, 1991).
Freedom is respected: faith cannot be forced (CCC 160).
quiz: According to Evangelii Nuntiandi, evangelization begins with…|Force|Silence|Witness of life, then proclamation|Debate|3|Paul VI, 1975.
Mission respects freedom because…|Faith cannot be coerced (CCC 160)|People do not matter|The Church is weak|It is easier|0|CCC 160.
Evangelization includes which four elements?|Fear, law, taxes, war|Debate, conquer, rule, ignore|Witness, proclamation, dialogue, charity|Study, wait, ask, vote|2|CCC 849–856 and Evangelii Gaudium.
lessons.life: Share your faith with someone.
lessons.saint: Paul Miki: a Japanese Jesuit who preached from the cross.
lessons.mem: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” (Matthew 28:19)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 28:19–20. Ask: “How have you met Christ through other people? Who evangelized you?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to define evangelization and name four forms.

script.open: Ask, “Think about a time someone tried to convince you of something. What worked? What made you shut down?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Church’s mission, from Jesus’ command in Matthew 28:19, is to evangelize. Paul VI wrote in Evangelii Nuntiandi: ‘Evangelizing is the grace and vocation proper to the Church, her deepest identity.’ Pope John Paul II called for a ‘new evangelization,’ new in ardor, methods and expression, to reach those who have drifted from the faith. Pope Francis in Evangelii Gaudium (2013) insists that the Gospel is joy and that every Christian is a missionary disciple. Evangelization has several aspects: witness of life, proclamation, conversion, entering the community, receiving sacraments and apostolate.”

Say: “Why do we do it? Because Christ commanded it. Because we want to share the gift of faith. Because God wants all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4). And because we believe the Gospel is true and the best news. How? The Church distinguishes among proclamation (the kerygma, the basic announcement that Jesus died and rose to save us), catechesis (teaching the faith), and apologetics (reasoned defense). The first message is: God loves you, Jesus died and rose for you, and he calls you to follow. Mission isn’t coercion: the Church respects freedom. Dignitatis Humanae: ‘The truth cannot impose itself except by the force of its own truth.’”

Say: “Evangelization involves inculturation: bringing the Gospel into the culture and letting it be expressed in local forms, as Ricci did in China and Cyril and Methodius among the Slavs. It also includes service of the poor and justice, as Jesus did. Today, mission fields are everywhere, including our neighborhoods. About a quarter of those raised Catholic in the U.S. have left the Church. Many are ‘nones’ with no religion. Good evangelization starts with listening, friendship and witness; it asks questions and invites; it avoids being pushy or argumentative. 1 Peter 3:15 says to be ready to give an account with gentleness and reverence. Francis said, ‘The Church grows not by proselytizing, but by attraction.’”
ask: What is the new evangelization? (Evangelization new in ardor, methods and expression, for those who have drifted.)
What is the kerygma? (The basic announcement of Jesus’ death and resurrection.)
What is inculturation? (Expressing the Gospel in local culture.)
practice: Write a two-minute story: one moment when your faith mattered.
Practice sharing it with a partner without arguing or pressuring.
Write three questions you would ask a friend who is not religious.
Plan one concrete invitation: Mass, a youth group, a service project.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, send me to those who need to hear your name.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Invite one person to something at your parish.”

tryit: Plan an invitation, not an argument.
Write your two-minute story.
Rehearse with a partner.
lessons.saintStory:
Paul Miki was born around 1562 in Japan, to a wealthy family. He was educated by Jesuits and became a Jesuit brother, a gifted preacher who brought many to the faith.
