Christianity had come to Japan with Francis Xavier in 1549 and had grown to hundreds of thousands. But in 1587 the ruler Hideyoshi began to fear the foreigners and ordered missionaries to leave.
In December 1596, he ordered the arrest of Christians in Kyoto and Osaka. Twenty-six were seized: six Franciscans, three Japanese Jesuits including Paul Miki, and seventeen lay Japanese, including three boys who were altar servers. They were marched about 600 miles through winter to Nagasaki. On February 5, 1597, they were crucified on a hill overlooking the city.
Paul Miki preached from his cross. “I am a Japanese by birth and a Brother of the Society of Jesus. I have committed no crime and the only reason why I am condemned to die is that I have been teaching the doctrine of our Lord Jesus Christ. I am very happy to die for such a reason.” He forgave his persecutors. After the martyrdoms, the Church in Japan survived underground for over 250 years.

lessons.title: Ecumenism and other religions
lessons.idea: The Church seeks unity among Christians and respects other religions. Nostra Aetate teaches that the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions, honors the Jewish people, esteems Muslims, and calls for dialogue and mutual respect.
lessons.question: How does the Church relate to others?
lessons.activity: “Respectful interfaith conversation” (40 min). Using guidelines for dialogue (listen, speak for yourself, ask honest questions), students prepare a conversation (possibly with a guest from another faith or Christian denomination). Afterwards they reflect: What did I learn? What do I still hold?
teach: Nostra Aetate (1965) says the Church “rejects nothing that is true and holy” in other religions (CCC 843). It calls for dialogue and collaboration.

The Jewish people remain beloved of God, “the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; CCC 839–840). Anti-Semitism is condemned. Muslims worship the one God and honor Jesus as prophet (CCC 841).
Christ is the one Mediator and the fullness of truth (CCC 846–848, 1 Timothy 2:5). Dialogue and evangelization are both authentic missions.
Ecumenical dialogue with other Christians seeks unity in truth (CCC 817–822).
talk: What do we share with Jews and Muslims?
How do we hold conviction and respect together?
quiz: Nostra Aetate teaches that the Church “rejects nothing that is true and holy” in other religions while…|Staying silent|Debating|Proclaiming Christ the way, the truth and the life (CCC 843)|Considering them identical|2|CCC 843.
Which is true of the Church’s relation to Judaism?|It avoids them|It condemns Jews|God’s covenant with the Jews is irrevocable (Romans 11:29; CCC 839–840)|It replaced Israel|2|CCC 839–840.
Good interreligious dialogue requires…|Honesty about one’s own beliefs and respect for others|Winning|Abandoning mission|Hiding beliefs|0|CCC 856.
lessons.life: Meet someone of another faith and listen.
lessons.saint: John Paul II: the pope who gathered the world’s religions to pray for peace at Assisi.
misc: “Respect for other faiths means weakening my own.”
lessons.mem: “I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word.” (John 17:20)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Do you have friends from other faiths? What did you learn from them?” Introduce the principle: respect without relativism.
lessons.assess: Ask students to state what Nostra Aetate teaches and give guidelines for dialogue.

script.open: Ask, “How do you talk with a friend whose religion is different? What do you share? What do you disagree about? How do you stay both honest and respectful?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Nostra Aetate (1965) is Vatican II’s declaration on non-Christian religions. It says: ‘The Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions.’ It looks at what we share. Judaism: our roots; God’s covenant with Israel has not been revoked; Jesus, Mary and the apostles were Jews; the Church condemns antisemitism. Islam: Muslims worship the one God, honor Jesus as a prophet, and Mary; the Council urges mutual understanding. Hinduism and Buddhism: they seek truth about the human condition and ways of liberation. Nostra Aetate also says the Church ‘proclaims, and ever must proclaim Christ, the way, the truth, and the life.’”

Say: “Ecumenism is the movement for unity among Christians. Unitatis Redintegratio (1964) says that all who are baptized are brothers and sisters in Christ, and that the Catholic Church is committed to restoring unity. We approach it by prayer, dialogue, shared service and study. Orthodox: close in sacraments and bishops; main differences are the Pope and the filioque. Protestants: share Scripture, Baptism and faith in Christ; differ on the Church’s authority, sacraments, and Mary. Ecumenism does not mean compromising doctrine, nor does it mean that all churches are equal. It means seeking the truth in charity. John Paul II said the Church must ‘breathe with both lungs.’”

Say: “Interreligious dialogue has four forms: the dialogue of life (living together), of action (working together for justice), of theological exchange, and of religious experience (sharing prayer and spirituality). Questions arise. Doesn’t this relativize Christ? No. The Church holds that Jesus is the unique Savior of all (Acts 4:12), and that the fullness of truth is found in Him. But she respects the dignity and freedom of each person. Pope Benedict XVI’s Regensburg lecture (2006) raised the matter of faith and violence. Today the Church works with Jewish and Muslim groups on charity and peace. The ‘Document on Human Fraternity’ (2019), signed by Pope Francis and the Grand Imam of al-Azhar, is an example.”
ask: What does Nostra Aetate say? (The Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions.)
What is ecumenism? (The movement for Christian unity.)
Does dialogue mean all religions are equal? (No; the Church holds Christ is the unique Savior.)
practice: Make a table: Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Orthodoxy, Protestantism. In each: what we share; what we differ on.
Add: one way Catholics can respectfully engage.
Write two sentences on what you must not give up in dialogue.
Plan one respectful question you could ask a friend of another faith.
script.close: Pray the Assisi prayer for peace or the Prayer of Saint Francis. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask a friend of another faith what they love about it.”

tryit: Match each approach to a church teaching.
Name what we share with each religion.
Write what we cannot give up.
lessons.saintStory:
Karol Wojtyła was born in 1920 in Wadowice, Poland. In his youth he loved theater, poetry and sport. During the German occupation, he worked in a quarry and chemical plant and secretly studied for the priesthood. He was ordained in 1946, became a professor and then archbishop of Kraków. In 1978 he was elected pope, the first non-Italian in 455 years.
He traveled to more than 120 countries. He was the first pope to visit a synagogue, in Rome in 1986, where he called Jews “our elder brothers.” In 2000, he prayed at the Western Wall in Jerusalem and left a note asking forgiveness. On October 27, 1986, in Assisi, he invited leaders of the world’s religions to pray for peace, each in their own way; this is sometimes misunderstood as syncretism, but he insisted that they came together to pray, not to pray together as one.
He wrote the encyclical Ut Unum Sint (1995) on Christian unity. He died in 2005 and was canonized in 2014.

lessons.title: Salvation and the Church
lessons.idea: “Outside the Church there is no salvation” means that all salvation comes from Christ through the Church, his Body. It does not mean that people who through no fault of their own do not know Christ are condemned. God desires all to be saved.
lessons.question: How are non-Catholics saved?
lessons.activity: “Study the text” (40 min). Students read CCC 846–848 and Lumen Gentium 14–16, and answer: What does the axiom mean? Who is saved? What obligations does the Church have? Write a short explanation to a friend who asks, “Do Catholics think everyone else is going to hell?”
teach: “All salvation comes from Christ the Head through the Church which is his Body” (CCC 846). Those who know the Church was founded by Christ and refuse to enter or remain cannot be saved (CCC 846).
Those who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel but seek God and do his will as they know it may be saved (CCC 847; Lumen Gentium 16). This is not indifferentism.
The Church’s mission is therefore more urgent, not less: “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel” (CCC 848; 1 Corinthians 9:16).
The Church does not declare anyone (except canonized saints) to be in heaven or hell.
quiz: “Outside the Church no salvation” means, per CCC 846,…|All salvation comes from Christ through the Church, his Body|The Church saves herself|All non-Catholics are lost|Only Catholics know God|0|CCC 846.

Who may be saved, according to CCC 847 and Lumen Gentium 16?|Only the rich|Only baptized Catholics|Those who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel but seek God and follow conscience|No one|2|CCC 847.

Why does this teaching make mission more urgent, not less?|It does not|Because Christ’s Church has the fullness of means and the commission to share them (CCC 848)|Mission is obsolete|No answer|1|CCC 848.
lessons.life: Write a paragraph explaining it to a friend.
lessons.saint: Cornelius the centurion: a God-fearing Roman soldier whom Peter baptized.
misc: “Catholics say all non-Catholics go to hell.”
lessons.mem: “God our Savior… desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” (1 Timothy 2:3–4)
lessons.hook: Read 1 Timothy 2:3–4. Ask: “If God wants everyone to be saved, how should we read ‘no salvation outside the Church’?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the axiom and its limits in a short paragraph.

script.open: Write the Latin phrase on the board: “Extra ecclesiam nulla salus”, and ask, “What do you think it means? Who might it condemn? Who might it include?” Take honest answers. “It is one of the most misunderstood phrases.”
teach: Say: “The Church teaches that Christ is the only Savior, and that the Church is necessary for salvation. ‘There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.’ (Acts 4:12) ‘Outside the Church there is no salvation’ goes back to Origen and Cyprian. The Catechism explains: ‘Basing itself on Scripture and Tradition, the Council teaches that the Church, a pilgrim now on earth, is necessary for salvation: the one Christ is the mediator and the way of salvation; he is present to us in his body which is the Church.’ (CCC 846) All salvation comes from Christ the Head through the Church, his Body.”

Say: “Yet it does not mean that only Catholics can be saved. The Council teaches, ‘Those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, but nevertheless seek God with a sincere heart, and, moved by grace, try in their actions to do his will as they know it through the dictates of their conscience—those too may achieve eternal salvation.’ (LG 16) Cornelius was such a person. Those who know that the Catholic Church was founded by Christ as necessary, and yet refuse to enter or remain in her, cannot be saved. Baptized non-Catholics are in imperfect communion. God’s grace works beyond the visible boundaries. Baptism of desire and baptism of blood are recognized.”

Say: “This leaves us two tasks. One, to proclaim Christ; the Church has an urgent mission since she has the fullness of the means of salvation. ‘Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel.’ (1 Corinthians 9:16) Two, to trust God’s mercy, who ‘desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.’ (1 Timothy 2:4) We do not judge the fate of any individual. We don’t know how many are saved. The Church has never declared that any particular person is in hell, not even Judas. And what about children who die unbaptized? The Church entrusts them to God’s mercy (CCC 1261); the International Theological Commission in 2007 gave reasons for hope. The Church’s teaching is balanced between universal salvific will and the necessity of Christ and the Church.”
ask: Is the Church necessary for salvation? (Yes; Christ saves through his Body, the Church.)
Can non-Catholics be saved? (Yes, if they sincerely seek God and live by conscience, through no fault of their own.)
Has the Church said anyone is in hell? (No.)
practice: Make a chart: What the Church teaches firmly / What the Church leaves to God’s mercy.
Fill in with items such as: Christ is the only Savior; the Church is necessary; sincere seekers can be saved; baptism of desire; unbaptized infants.
Write a careful reply to a friend who says, ‘So you think everyone else is going to hell?’
Practice saying it kindly.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, you desire all to be saved. Bring everyone to you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for someone far from God by name.”

tryit: Sort teachings on salvation: what the Church holds firmly.
Mark what the Church leaves to God.
Write a careful reply to a friend.
lessons.saintStory:
Cornelius was a centurion in the Roman army, stationed at Caesarea, in the Italian Cohort. He was a devout man who feared God, gave alms generously and prayed constantly. One afternoon, an angel appeared and said, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. Send men to Joppa for Simon, who is called Peter.”
Meanwhile, Peter had a vision of a sheet descending with all kinds of animals, and a voice said, “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” He objected, as many were unclean by Jewish law. The voice said, “What God has cleansed, you must not call common.” When Cornelius’s messengers arrived, Peter understood. He went to Cornelius’s house, though entering a Gentile home was forbidden for Jews. He said, “Truly I perceive that God shows no partiality, but in every nation any one who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.”
While Peter was preaching, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard, and he baptized them. Cornelius was the first Gentile convert in Acts.

lessons.title: Infallibility
lessons.idea: Christ gave the Church the gift of infallibility so that she can teach definitively on faith and morals without error. The Pope, and the bishops in union with him, exercise it in precise circumstances, not in every statement.
lessons.question: What is infallible?
lessons.activity: “Write a summary” (35 min). Students read CCC 889–892 and Lumen Gentium 25, then write a one-page summary answering: What is infallibility? Who has it? When is it exercised? What it is not (impeccability, omniscience)? Give two examples of definitions (Nicaea; Assumption, 1950).
teach: Infallibility is the gift by which “the Church’s Magisterium … enjoys … the supreme charism of infallibility in matters of faith and morals” (CCC 890–891).

It is exercised by (1) the Pope speaking ex cathedra, (2) the college of bishops with the Pope in an ecumenical council, and (3) the ordinary and universal Magisterium when bishops agree on a point to be held definitively (CCC 891–892).
It does not mean the Pope is sinless or always right. Pastoral decisions can be wrong.
Vatican I (1870) defined papal infallibility; it is rarely exercised. The faithful also have an infallibility in believing (sensus fidei, CCC 92).
quiz: Papal infallibility applies when the Pope…|Speaks on any subject|Gives an interview|Defines a doctrine on faith or morals to be held by the whole Church (CCC 891)|Writes a letter|2|CCC 891.
Infallibility does not mean…|The Church is guided|The Pope cannot sin|The Spirit helps|The Pope teaches truth under conditions|1|It does not mean impeccability.
Which dogma was defined ex cathedra in 1950?|The Assumption of Mary|The Resurrection|The Trinity|The Real Presence|0|Pius XII.
lessons.life: List defined dogmas.
lessons.saint: Peter: the one for whom Jesus prayed that his faith would not fail.
lessons.mem: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth.” (John 16:13)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Could a guide be right every time on a particular point without being right about everything?” Read John 16:13: “He will guide you into all the truth.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to state three conditions for ex cathedra teaching and what infallibility does not mean.

script.open: Ask, “Can a person who is flawed be trusted to teach truth? What would give you confidence?” Take answers. “That is the question infallibility answers.”
teach: Say: “Infallibility is the gift by which the Church cannot err in teaching what must be believed about faith or morals. It rests on Christ’s promises: ‘the gates of hell shall not prevail against it’ (Matthew 16:18); ‘I will pray the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, to be with you for ever, the Spirit of truth’ (John 14:16-17); ‘The Spirit of truth will guide you into all the truth.’ (John 16:13) If Christ founded the Church to teach, and if she could teach error about salvation, she would be useless. Paul calls the Church ‘the pillar and bulwark of the truth.’ (1 Timothy 3:15)”

Say: “Vatican I (1870) defined papal infallibility: ‘when he speaks ex cathedra, that is, when in discharge of the office of pastor and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole Church,’ he possesses that infallibility with which Christ willed his Church to be endowed. Conditions: he speaks as pastor of all; on faith or morals; definitively; intending to bind the whole Church. Examples: the Immaculate Conception (Pius IX, 1854) and the Assumption (Pius XII, 1950). Ex cathedra definitions are very rare. Infallibility also belongs to the whole Church (the body of the faithful), and to the college of bishops in union with the Pope (e.g., in an ecumenical council or by the ordinary universal Magisterium).”

Say: “What infallibility is not. It doesn’t mean impeccability (the Pope is a sinner and goes to confession). It doesn’t mean the Pope is inspired (the Holy Spirit assists but does not give new revelation). It doesn’t cover everything he says: his opinions on science, politics or history, his homilies and interviews, his prudential decisions. It doesn’t mean there haven’t been bad popes: some were bad men, yet none officially taught heresy in an ex cathedra definition. Critics point to Honorius, Galileo and the Inquisition. The Church’s response: Honorius did not define a doctrine; the Galileo case was a disciplinary decision of a Roman congregation, not an ex cathedra definition. The charism protects the content of the faith, not the personal wisdom of every pope.”
ask: Who prayed that Peter’s faith not fail? (Jesus.)
What are conditions for ex cathedra teaching? (As pastor of all, on faith or morals, definitively, to bind the whole Church.)
Does infallibility mean the Pope can’t sin? (No.)
practice: Prepare cards of statements: a Pope’s statement on climate policy; the definition of the Assumption; a Pope’s homily; the Nicene Creed; an encyclical on social justice.
Sort into infallible, authoritative but not infallible, and personal opinion.
Write the condition that decides each.
Write a one-paragraph reply to someone who says ‘Catholics think the Pope can’t be wrong about anything.’
script.close: Pray: “Lord, keep your Church in the truth.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for the Pope by name.”

tryit: Sort statements into infallible and not.
Cite the condition for each.
Explain what infallibility is not.
lessons.saintStory:
At the Last Supper, as the disciples argued about who was the greatest, Jesus turned to Simon: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you all like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brethren.” Peter protested that he was ready to go to prison and death with Jesus. Jesus said, “I tell you, Peter, the cock will not crow this day, until you three times deny that you know me.”
Hours later, in the courtyard of the high priest, Peter denied him three times. The cock crowed, and the Lord turned and looked at Peter. Peter went out and wept bitterly. After the Resurrection, on the shore of Galilee, Jesus asked him three times, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” and three times commissioned him: “Feed my lambs… Tend my sheep… Feed my sheep.”
The man who failed was the man who was given the keys. The Church sees in Peter’s story that infallibility is a gift of Christ’s prayer, not a sign of Peter’s own strength.

lessons.title: Conscience and teaching
lessons.idea: Conscience is the inner judgment of reason about right and wrong. It must be formed, and a well-formed Catholic conscience is formed by Scripture, the teaching of the Church, prayer and honest reflection. We must always follow a certain conscience, and we must work to inform it.
lessons.question: How do we form conscience?
lessons.activity: “Case study” (35 min). Present a case where a student feels pressure (e.g., an invitation to a party with serious temptation; a school assignment that requires copying; a dilemma about telling the truth). Walk through the steps: gather facts, pray, consult Church teaching and trusted advisors, consider consequences, decide, reflect. Discuss.
teach: Conscience binds in the moment, and must be well formed (CCC 1783–1785). “A human being must always obey the certain judgment of his conscience” (CCC 1790), but conscience can err through ignorance (CCC 1790–1794).

The Church’s teaching is a source of light for conscience (CCC 2039). “In the formation of conscience the Word of God is the light for our path” (CCC 1785). Catholics owe the Magisterium a docile hearing.
Conscience is not “whatever I feel.” It is a judgment of reason about the truth.
Cardinal Newman: conscience is “the aboriginal Vicar of Christ.” His toast: “I shall drink to the Pope, if you please — still, to Conscience first, and to the Pope afterwards.” Read in full context.
quiz: A person must follow conscience but also…|Never doubt|Ignore Church teaching|Form it by Scripture, Church teaching and prayer (CCC 1783–1785)|Avoid questions|2|CCC 1783–1785.
Which best describes a well-formed Catholic conscience?|Majority opinion|Habit|A judgment of reason informed by truth and the Church’s teaching (CCC 1778, 2039)|Whatever feels right|2|CCC 1778, 2039.
Erroneous conscience can be culpable when…|Always|Never|Only for atheists|Ignorance results from neglecting to seek the truth (CCC 1791)|3|CCC 1791.
lessons.life: Read CCC 1776–1802.
lessons.saint: Thomas Becket: an archbishop who put conscience and the Church before the king.
misc: “Following my conscience means I can ignore Church teaching.”
lessons.mem: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind.” (Romans 12:2)
lessons.hook: Read Romans 12:2. Ask: “What does it mean to be ‘transformed by the renewal of your mind’?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how to form conscience with a short case.

script.open: Say, “You are given an order by someone with power over you. You believe it is wrong. What do you do?” Take answers. “This is the problem of conscience and authority.”
teach: Say: “Conscience is the inner judgment of reason that a particular act is right or wrong. The Catechism: ‘Moral conscience, present at the heart of the person, enjoins him at the appropriate moment to do good and to avoid evil.’ (CCC 1777) Vatican II: ‘In the depths of his conscience, man detects a law which he does not impose upon himself, but which holds him to obedience. Its voice… tells him to love and to do what is good and to avoid evil.’ (GS 16) ‘A man has the right to act in conscience and in freedom so as personally to make moral decisions. He must not be forced to act contrary to his conscience.’ (CCC 1782) So we must always follow our conscience, even a mistaken one, if sincere.”

Say: “But conscience must be formed. It is not simply feelings or opinions. John Henry Newman: conscience is ‘the aboriginal Vicar of Christ,’ but not self-will. He wrote that he would toast ‘to conscience first, and to the Pope afterwards,’ meaning a well-formed conscience. The Church teaches that the Catholic faithful ‘must carefully attend to the sacred and certain doctrine of the Church’ in forming conscience. (Dignitatis Humanae 14) The Church’s teaching authority doesn’t replace conscience; it informs it. When the Church teaches on faith and morals, a Catholic should give assent. If one struggles, one should study, pray, and consult a wise priest or teacher, not simply decide against the Church.”

Say: “What about a conflict? Conscience can be erroneous: invincibly (through no fault of one’s own), when the person is not culpable; or vincibly, when it results from negligence or sin. We are responsible for forming it well. Conscience can be formed by Scripture, the Magisterium, prayer, advice, examination. It can be deadened by habitual sin. A moral decision involves three sources: the object, the intention and the circumstances. Some acts are intrinsically evil: always wrong, regardless of intention. A good intention does not justify an evil means. Becket and More acted from well-formed conscience in conflict with civil law. We should speak of ‘conscientious objection’ in medicine, military service and so on; the Church supports it.”
ask: What does the Church teach about following conscience? (Always follow it, but form it well.)
Can conscience be mistaken? (Yes, and we are responsible for forming it.)
What are the three sources of morality? (Object, intention, circumstances.)
practice: Present a case: a nurse is asked to assist in an act the Church teaches is gravely wrong.
Work through: What is the act? What does the Church teach? What are my options? What advice do I need? What would a well-formed conscience decide?
Write your response.
Discuss how conscience relates to law, work and loyalty.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, give me a well-formed conscience and courage to act on it.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Examine your conscience nightly this week.”

tryit: Work out a case with the steps of conscience.
Find where the Church’s teaching enters.
Decide and defend.
lessons.saintStory:
Thomas Becket was born in London around 1118, the son of a merchant. He became a clerk, then the chancellor of England, and a close friend of King Henry II. They hunted, feasted and worked together. In 1162, Henry made him archbishop of Canterbury, hoping he would serve royal interests in the Church.
The change surprised everyone. Thomas gave up his luxury and took up a simple life of prayer and penance. He refused to agree to the king’s Constitutions of Clarendon, which would have placed the clergy under royal courts. The quarrel grew bitter. Thomas fled to France for six years. He returned in 1170 after a truce.
Henry, in a fit of anger, is said to have exclaimed, “Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?” Four knights went to Canterbury and killed Thomas in the cathedral on December 29, 1170, as he was walking into evening prayer. Henry did public penance at Thomas’s tomb. Thomas was canonized in 1173.

lessons.title: Dissent, doubt and reform
lessons.idea: The Church, holy yet made of sinners, always needs renewal. The saints reform from within, through love and obedience: Francis rebuilt the Church by living the Gospel, Catherine of Siena called popes to fidelity, Teresa reformed Carmel, Charles Borromeo reformed his diocese.
lessons.question: How do saints reform?
lessons.activity: “Reformers study” (40 min). Pairs study Francis, Catherine, Teresa or Borromeo. They answer: What was wrong? What did they do? How did they remain faithful? Compare them with those who left. Discuss: What kind of reform is genuine?
teach: “The Church … is at once holy and always in need of purification, and follows constantly the path of penance and renewal” (CCC 827; Lumen Gentium 8).

Genuine reform comes from holiness, not from rejecting authority. The saints show the way: Francis rebuilt San Damiano; Catherine wrote to Gregory XI; Teresa insisted on a return to prayer; Borromeo reformed clergy.
Today the Church speaks of ongoing conversion, accountability and the call to holiness (CCC 1428). Students have a part to play.
Honest dissent is different from sustained opposition. The Church encourages respectful questions and prayer.
talk: What is the right response to scandal?
quiz: The Church is “holy and always in need of purification” (CCC 827). This means…|She cannot change|She is invisible|She is holy in Christ yet her members need repentance and reform|She is corrupt|2|CCC 827.
Which saint “rebuilt my church” by living the Gospel?|Francis of Assisi|Constantine|Charlemagne|Luther|0|San Damiano.

A genuine reformer in the Church differs from a schismatic in that…|He has no followers|He loves power|He is quieter|He seeks renewal in fidelity and communion|3|Examples: Catherine, Teresa, Borromeo.
lessons.life: Pray for the Church’s renewal.
lessons.saint: Alphonsus Liguori: a lawyer who found the path between harshness and laxity.
lessons.mem: “Let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely… looking to Jesus.” (Hebrews 12:1–2)
lessons.hook: Read Hebrews 12:1–2. Ask: “How can the Church be both holy and sinful?” Introduce the phrase “always in need of purification” (CCC 827).
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe a saint’s reform and what it shows.

script.open: Ask, “What is the difference between asking a hard question and rejecting an answer? Between criticizing a friend and betraying a friend?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Catholics can have difficulties with Church teaching. The Catechism distinguishes. Doubt: honest difficulty in understanding or believing. Involuntary doubt isn’t a sin; voluntary doubt, if deliberately encouraged, is. The father in Mark 9:24 prays, ‘I believe; help my unbelief!’ Questions are part of the search: Thomas Aquinas began each article with objections. Dissent: publicly rejecting a defined teaching. Heresy is the obstinate denial or doubt after Baptism of a truth to be believed with divine and Catholic faith. Different from dissent are theological questions raised to deepen understanding.”

Say: “The Church asks different levels of assent. For dogmas: the assent of faith. For definitive teachings: firm acceptance. For authoritative non-definitive teaching: ‘religious submission of mind and will’ (LG 25), which is a presumption in favor, with room for serious study. The Church distinguishes between a legitimate theological discussion and public dissent that undermines the faith of others. In 1990, the instruction Donum Veritatis addressed the vocation of theologians: they serve the Church, and difficulties should be raised privately and respectfully with Church authorities. Silencing has happened too: some theologians, like Yves Congar and John Courtney Murray, were censored in the 1950s, and later vindicated at Vatican II. So the Church does recognize that questioning has led to growth.”

Say: “Reform. The Church is always in need of reform (ecclesia semper reformanda). How? By the saints: Francis, Dominic, Catherine of Siena, Teresa of Avila, Ignatius, Charles Borromeo, Alphonsus. Not by tearing the Church down, but by holiness, charity and fidelity, speaking the truth with love. Catherine rebuked the pope, but kneeling. Her love for the Church was clear. If we see problems, we should pray, study, speak respectfully to those in authority, support good causes, and keep our own lives holy. Newman, Congar and de Lubac suffered misunderstanding but remained faithful. The Church has also reformed discipline: the liturgy, canon law, the handling of abuse. Reform strengthens; dissent can divide.”
ask: What is the difference between doubt and dissent? (Doubt is an honest difficulty; dissent is public rejection of a teaching.)
What level of assent does non-definitive teaching call for? (Religious submission of mind and will.)
How have saints reformed the Church? (By holiness, charity and fidelity.)
practice: Prepare cases: a student struggles with a teaching; a theologian publishes a dissenting article; a parish group wants the Church to change a discipline; a saint rebukes a bishop in a letter.
Rate each: faithful questioning, dissent, or reform.
Write what you would do if you struggled with a teaching.
Share with a partner.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, renew your Church, beginning with me.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Write down a hard question and find a wise person to discuss it.”

tryit: Distinguish dissent, doubt and loyal questioning.
Mark acceptable responses.
Write what faithful reform looks like.
lessons.saintStory:
Alphonsus Liguori was born in 1696 in Naples, to a noble family. He became a lawyer at sixteen, with a brilliant career. In 1723, he lost a major case, due to missing a document, and was so humiliated that he left the law. He became a priest in 1726 and worked among the poor of Naples. In 1732, he founded the Redemptorists, to preach to abandoned country people.
He saw that confessors were tangled in two errors: rigorism (making the moral law impossibly heavy, driving people away) and laxism (excusing everything). He wrote a Moral Theology that took a sensible, pastoral middle way, always looking for the truth but remembering that confession was a hospital, not a court. His principle: when the law truly doubtful, the person is free.
He was named bishop at sixty-six and spent his last years in pain, and wrote many books, including The Glories of Mary and Visits to the Blessed Sacrament. He died in 1787 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1871. He is the patron of confessors and moral theologians.

lessons.title: Mary in the plan of salvation
lessons.idea: Mary has a unique role in God’s plan: Mother of God, ever-virgin, immaculate from her conception and assumed body and soul into heaven. The Church honors her because of her Son and sees in her the model of faith and the image of the Church.
lessons.question: Why four Marian dogmas?
lessons.activity: “Biblical foundations of Marian teaching” (40 min). Students map each dogma to Scripture and Tradition: Mother of God (Luke 1:43; Ephesus 431), Immaculate Conception (Luke 1:28; Genesis 3:15; 1854), perpetual virginity (Luke 1:34; Ezekiel 44:2; Lateran 649), Assumption (Revelation 12; 1950). Discuss how each points to Christ.
teach: Mary is the Mother of God (Theotokos) because her Son is God (CCC 495). She is ever-virgin (CCC 499–507) and immaculate (CCC 490–493).
The Assumption (1950) is the final fulfilment of her union with her Son (CCC 966). She is a type of the Church (CCC 967–970) and our spiritual mother (John 19:26–27).
Devotion to Mary is “intrinsically included” in Christian worship but is different from adoration (CCC 971). The Rosary, Marian feasts and consecrations aim at Christ.
Give attention to how Protestant students may respond; explain without defensiveness.
quiz: “Theotokos” means…|Mother of God, literally God-bearer|Mother of the Church|Mother of the faithful|Queen of heaven|0|CCC 495.
The Immaculate Conception refers to…|The virgin birth|Her Assumption|Jesus’ conception|Mary being preserved from original sin from her conception|3|CCC 490–493.
Catholics distinguish veneration of Mary (hyperdulia) from…|Respect|Adoration (latria), which is due to God alone (CCC 971)|Love|Imitation|1|CCC 971.
lessons.life: Pray a Rosary.
lessons.saint: Louis de Montfort: a preacher who taught that the shortest way to Jesus is through Mary.
misc: “Mary is a co-redeemer in the same sense as Christ.”
lessons.mem: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!” (Luke 1:42)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 1:26–56. Ask: “What do Gabriel, Elizabeth and Mary herself say about her?” List them.
lessons.assess: Ask students to state the four Marian dogmas and one biblical clue for each.

script.open: Ask, “Why do Catholics honor Mary so much? Some say it takes away from Jesus. How would you answer?” Take answers. “Let’s see how the doctrine is built.”
teach: Say: “Mary is central to Catholic faith because of who her Son is. All Marian doctrines are ultimately about Christ. There are four Marian dogmas. One: Mary is the Mother of God (Theotokos), defined at Ephesus in 431. Luke 1:43: Elizabeth calls her ‘the mother of my Lord.’ Two: Mary’s perpetual virginity: before, during and after the birth of Christ (Lateran 649). Isaiah 7:14; Luke 1:34. Three: the Immaculate Conception: Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception, in view of Christ’s merits (Pius IX, 1854). The angel calls her ‘full of grace,’ kecharitomene (Luke 1:28). Four: the Assumption: at the end of her life, she was taken body and soul into heavenly glory (Pius XII, 1950).”

Say: “The ‘brothers of the Lord’ in the Gospels: the Church understands them as relatives, because the Greek word and Hebrew ‘ach’ can mean cousin, and the Gospels do not call them Mary’s sons. Mary’s title ‘New Eve’ is found in Irenaeus and Justin. Her role at Cana (John 2) shows her intercession. In Revelation 12, the woman clothed with the sun is read as Mary and the Church. The Church distinguishes veneration (hyperdulia, special honor) given to Mary, from adoration (latria), given to God alone. Catholics do not worship Mary. Mary points to Jesus: ‘Do whatever he tells you.’ (John 2:5)”

Say: “Lumen Gentium chapter 8 places Mary in the mystery of Christ and the Church. She is Mother of the Church (Paul VI, 1964) and the model disciple. She prays for us as our spiritual mother. At the cross, Jesus said to John, ‘Behold, your mother.’ Marian devotions include the Rosary, the Angelus, the Memorare, the Litany of Loreto, the scapular and consecration. Marian apparitions such as Guadalupe, Lourdes and Fatima are approved as worthy of belief but are not required. The Church’s greatest Marian writing is the Magnificat, Mary’s own song (Luke 1:46-55). Louis de Montfort’s motto: ‘Ad Jesum per Mariam’, to Jesus through Mary.”
ask: Name the four Marian dogmas. (Mother of God, perpetual virginity, Immaculate Conception, Assumption.)
What is the difference between veneration and adoration? (Veneration is honor; adoration is for God alone.)
What does Mary always point to? (Jesus.)
practice: Make a table of the four dogmas: statement, Bible text, date defined, what it says about Christ.
Add the Magnificat and underline two lines.
Write a short reply to a friend who says Catholics worship Mary.
Pray the Memorare.
script.close: Pray the Memorare together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray the Rosary with your family.”

tryit: Trace the four Marian dogmas to their sources.
Write the Scripture behind each.
Explain why each is about Christ.
lessons.saintStory:
Louis-Marie Grignion was born in 1673 in Brittany, France. He was ordained in 1700, and became a wandering missionary, preaching in villages and cities, often in the open air and in poverty. He was sometimes banned from preaching in a diocese because of opposition. He rebuilt chapels, taught the Rosary, set up schools, and composed hymns.
In about 1712, he wrote True Devotion to Mary, which taught total consecration to Jesus through Mary: giving oneself entirely to Jesus by giving oneself to his mother. The manuscript was hidden in a chest, and not found until 1842. It has since become a classic and influenced Pope John Paul II, whose motto, Totus Tuus, comes from it.
He founded the Company of Mary and the Daughters of Wisdom. He died in 1716, at forty-three, and was canonized in 1947. His central point: Marian devotion exists to lead us to Christ.

lessons.title: The communion of saints
lessons.idea: The communion of saints unites the Church on earth, the souls in purgatory and the saints in heaven. We can ask the saints to pray for us just as we ask friends, because those who live in Christ are not separated by death. Scripture supports this.
lessons.question: Why ask saints for prayers?
lessons.activity: “Respond to an objection” (35 min). Students prepare answers to: “Praying to saints replaces Christ”; “The dead cannot hear us”; “Intercessory prayer is idolatry.” Evidence: Revelation 5:8 (elders offering prayers), Hebrews 12:1, Luke 16:19–31, Luke 20:38, Matthew 17 (Moses and Elijah), James 5:16. Role-play a respectful conversation.
teach: The communion of saints includes the pilgrim Church, the Church suffering and the Church triumphant (CCC 946–962). The saints’ prayers are heard (CCC 956–957).

We distinguish latria (worship, due to God alone), dulia (veneration of saints), hyperdulia (special honor to Mary) (CCC 971). “There is one mediator” (1 Timothy 2:5) but we share in his mediation as members of his Body.
The Church canonizes with certainty that the person is in heaven (CCC 828). The process includes miracles for beatification and canonization.
Address the practice of prayer for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:45–46; CCC 1032).
talk: How does it relate to Christ’s unique mediation?
quiz: Which text shows heavenly beings offering the prayers of the saints?|Revelation 5:8|Genesis 3|Psalm 51|Romans 1|0|Revelation 5:8.
The communion of saints includes…|The Church on earth, the souls being purified and the saints in heaven (CCC 954)|Only clergy|Only the dead|Only the holy|0|CCC 954.
Asking the saints to pray for us is analogous to…|Asking fellow Christians to pray (James 5:16)|Ancestor worship|Magic|Fortune telling|0|CCC 956–957.
lessons.life: Ask a saint for prayer for a specific need.
lessons.saint: Anthony of Padua: a preacher whom people trust to help them find what is lost.
misc: “Asking saints for help detracts from Jesus.”
lessons.mem: “Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses… let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us.” (Hebrews 12:1)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Do you ask people to pray for you?” Everyone does. “Is death a barrier to the Body of Christ?” Read Hebrews 12:1.
lessons.assess: Ask students to respond to one objection about prayer to the saints with biblical evidence.

script.open: Ask, “Have you ever asked a friend to pray for you? Why do we do that? Do you think it helps? Does death end that friendship?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Church is one family in three states: the Church militant or pilgrim, on earth; the Church suffering, those in purgatory being purified; and the Church triumphant, the saints in heaven. We are united by love. The Catechism says: ‘We believe in the communion of all the faithful of Christ, those who are pilgrims on earth, the dead who are being purified, and the blessed in heaven, all together forming one Church.’ (CCC 962) Death does not break the bonds. Hebrews 12:1: ‘We are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses.’ The saints in heaven are alive in Christ. Jesus said, ‘God is not God of the dead, but of the living.’”

Say: “Why do Catholics ask the saints to pray? The same reason we ask friends: James 5:16, ‘The prayer of a righteous man has great power in its effects.’ In Revelation 5:8, the elders offer the prayers of the saints before the Lamb. In 2 Maccabees 15:12-14, Jeremiah prays for the people after his death. At the Transfiguration, Moses and Elijah talk with Jesus. The saints don’t replace Christ as mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), but share in his intercession as members of his body. We pray to God and ask the saints to pray with us. Veneration of saints is not worship. We honor them, imitate them, and ask their prayers. We use statues and icons as reminders, as people use photographs.”

Say: “Purgatory is the state of purification after death for those who die in God’s friendship but not yet fully purified. 1 Corinthians 3:15 speaks of being saved ‘as through fire.’ The Church prays for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:45-46). We pray for the dead at Mass, on All Souls’ Day (November 2), and we can offer indulgences, Masses and good works. An indulgence is the remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sin whose guilt has already been forgiven; it is granted by the Church under certain conditions. The saints are canonized after a process: a Servant of God, then Venerable, then Blessed (after a miracle), then Saint (after a second miracle; martyrs need none for beatification). Canonization is an infallible declaration that the person is in heaven and can be venerated.”
ask: What are the three parts of the Church? (Pilgrim on earth, suffering in purgatory, triumphant in heaven.)
Why ask the saints to pray? (Same as asking friends; they are alive in Christ.)
What is canonization? (A declaration that a person is in heaven.)
practice: Draw a diagram of the three states of the Church with arrows of prayer between them.
Choose a saint for a particular need and write a prayer asking for their help.
Look up the steps from Servant of God to Saint, and write them.
Pray for someone who has died.
script.close: Pray the Litany of the Saints (a few invocations) or “Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for your deceased relatives by name.”

tryit: Explain the three parts of the Church: pilgrim, suffering, triumphant.
Describe how the saints help us.
Write a prayer asking a saint for help.
lessons.saintStory:
Fernando was born in 1195 in Lisbon, to a noble family. At fifteen he joined the Augustinian canons, and studied the Bible. When the bodies of five Franciscan friars martyred in Morocco were brought to Portugal in 1220, he was moved, and he joined the Franciscans, taking the name Anthony. He wanted to go to Morocco himself, but fell ill and was shipped back, and landed in Sicily.
His gifts were hidden until, at an ordination, no one else was prepared to preach, and Anthony was asked. He spoke with such depth that Francis of Assisi appointed him to teach his friars. He then preached across Italy and southern France, drawing huge crowds, especially against heresy. He was called the “Hammer of Heretics,” and was known for tenderness to the poor.
He died in 1231 at thirty-six and was canonized within a year. A popular story says a novice took his psalter and ran off; Anthony prayed, and the novice returned it, which is why he is invoked to find lost things.

lessons.title: Heroes of faith
lessons.idea: Hebrews 11 lists heroes of faith, and the Church honors saints in every age and state of life — martyrs, mystics, teachers, parents, kids, laborers. Holiness is not just for the extraordinary; it is the vocation of every baptized person.
lessons.question: Who inspires you?
lessons.activity: “Present on a saint” (40 min). Each student presents a saint from a different state of life (a young person: Carlo Acutis, Maria Goretti; a parent: Gianna Molla, Louis and Zélie Martin; a worker: Joseph; a scholar: Edith Stein; a missionary: Katharine Drexel). Include a quote, a challenge and a prayer.
teach: The universal call to holiness (Lumen Gentium 39–42; CCC 2013) means all are called to “the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of charity.”
The canonization process: servant of God, venerable, blessed (beatified after a miracle), saint (after a second miracle, except for martyrs) (CCC 828).
The saints show many styles of holiness; their feast days teach the liturgical year. They are friends and models, and “icons” of Christ.
Encourage students to find a patron saint and learn their story.
talk: How do saints show holiness in ordinary life?
quiz: The universal call to holiness (Lumen Gentium 39–42) says…|All the faithful, in every state, are called to the fullness of Christian life (CCC 2013)|Only martyrs are called|Only clergy are called|Only monks|0|CCC 2013.
For canonization a miracle is generally required after…|Birth|Baptism|Beatification and, again, for canonization (martyrs excepted for beatification)|Ordination|2|CCC 828 context.
Which saint is a modern young person canonized for holiness in ordinary life?|Aquinas|Augustine|Carlo Acutis|Jerome|2|Carlo Acutis (canonized 2025).
lessons.life: Research and present on a saint.
lessons.saint: Titus Brandsma: a Dutch Carmelite professor who defended the free press and died at Dachau.
misc: “Holiness is for monks and nuns, not for ordinary people.”
lessons.mem: “Be holy, for I am holy.” (1 Peter 1:16)
lessons.hook: Read Hebrews 11:1–2 and 11:32–40. Ask: “What do these heroes have in common?” They trusted God though they did not see the full promise.
lessons.assess: Ask students to present a saint and one practical lesson they draw from the saint.

script.open: Ask, “Who is a person in history or today that you admire for standing up when it was costly? What did they do?” Take answers.
teach: Read Hebrews 11. Say: “This chapter is a roll call of heroes of faith. ‘By faith Abel offered… By faith Noah… By faith Abraham obeyed… By faith Moses… Rahab… and what more shall I say? Time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets.’ Then comes the point: ‘Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus the pioneer and perfecter of our faith.’ (Hebrews 12:1-2)”

Say: “The Church honors heroes of faith in each age. In the early Church, martyrs. In the Middle Ages, monks and mystics. In the modern age, missionaries, founders, workers for the poor. In the twentieth century, martyrs under Nazism and Communism: Maximilian Kolbe, Edith Stein, Titus Brandsma, Franz Jägerstätter, Cardinal Mindszenty, Oscar Romero, and the martyrs of Mexico. John Paul II said the twentieth century had more Christian martyrs than any before. Heroes also include ordinary people: Pier Giorgio Frassati, Carlo Acutis, Chiara Badano, Gianna Molla, Josemaría. Holiness in every state and every age.”

Say: “What makes a hero of faith? Not perfection, but love of Christ and others, perseverance, and trust. The saints had flaws; Paul persecuted Christians, Augustine lived badly, Peter denied Jesus. They were changed by grace. Pope Francis wrote in Gaudete et Exsultate (2018) about ‘the saints next door’: ‘the middle class of holiness.’ Saints in the Beatitudes: poor in spirit, meek, merciful, peacemakers. The call to holiness is yours. Leon Bloy said, ‘The only real sadness, the only real failure, the only great tragedy in life, is not to become a saint.’ Whose example will you follow?”
ask: What does Hebrews 11 describe? (Heroes of faith from the Old Testament.)
Name a modern martyr. (Kolbe, Brandsma, Romero, Stein.)
What does Francis call ordinary holiness? (The saints next door.)
practice: Read Hebrews 11 in a group, each taking a verse.
On a sheet, make your own roll call with five saints or heroes you know, and a line for what each risked.
Add one living person who inspires you.
Write one thing you can imitate.
script.close: Pray the Litany of the Saints or “All you holy men and women, pray for us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read the life of a saint this week.”

tryit: Read Hebrews 11 and make your own roll call.
Write what each hero risked.
Add a modern hero.
lessons.saintStory:
Titus Brandsma was born in 1881 in the Netherlands, in a farming family. He became a Carmelite priest, a philosopher and professor at the Catholic University of Nijmegen, and a journalist. He was known for his sense of humor, his devotion to Mary and his kindness.
When the Nazis occupied the Netherlands in 1940, they pressured the Catholic press to publish Nazi propaganda. Titus, as the bishops’ adviser to Catholic journalists, traveled from newspaper to newspaper urging editors to refuse. He was arrested in January 1942 and held in prison, then sent to Dachau concentration camp.
There he was beaten and experimented on. Even so, he kept up the spirits of fellow prisoners and forgave his guards. A nurse who gave him the lethal injection in July 1942 was given a rosary by him, and wrote later that she was moved by his kindness. On his prison wall he left a note: “Let us pray for those who persecute us.” He died on July 26, 1942, and was canonized in 2022.

units.title: Living the Paschal Mystery
units.eq: How does Christ’s death and rising shape our life?

lessons.title: Dying and rising in Baptism
lessons.idea: In Baptism we die and rise with Christ. Immersed in the water, we are buried with him in death and raised to new life, receiving forgiveness of sin and adoption as God’s children. Baptism begins the Christian life.
lessons.question: What does baptism do?
lessons.activity: “Study the rite” (40 min). Walk through the Rite of Baptism or the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults: signing, anointing, water, white garment, candle. Students explain each sign and gesture in relation to dying and rising. Compare with the Easter Vigil renewal of baptismal promises.
teach: Baptism incorporates us into Christ’s death and Resurrection (CCC 1214–1222, 1227). The Fathers saw the Red Sea and the Jordan as types (CCC 1217–1222).
Effects: forgiveness of original and personal sin, new birth as children of God, membership in Christ’s Body, an indelible character (CCC 1262–1274).
Ordinary minister: bishop, priest, deacon; in emergencies anyone, with water and the Trinitarian formula (CCC 1256). Baptism of desire and blood are recognized (CCC 1258–1260).
Infant Baptism is based on the Church’s practice from apostolic times (CCC 1250–1252).
talk: How does Baptism unite us to Christ’s death and resurrection?
quiz: Romans 6:3–4 compares Baptism to…|A wedding|A school|Burial with Christ and rising to new life|A bath only|2|CCC 1214.
Baptism of blood refers to…|A symbol|Martyrdom for Christ before Baptism (CCC 1258)|Anointing|Sacrifice of animals|1|CCC 1258.
The indelible character of Baptism means…|It ends sin|It is private|It can be repeated|It marks the soul permanently, so it is not repeated (CCC 1272)|3|CCC 1272.
lessons.life: Renew baptismal promises.
lessons.saint: Philip the Evangelist: the deacon who baptized the Ethiopian on a desert road.
misc: “Infants shouldn’t be baptized because they can’t choose.”
lessons.mem: “We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.” (Romans 6:4)
lessons.hook: Read Romans 6:3–11. Ask: “Why would Paul use death and burial language for a washing?” Show a picture of ancient baptisteries shaped like tombs.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Romans 6:3–11 in their own words and the effects of Baptism.

script.open: Ask, “What do you think the eunuch felt coming up out of the water? Why did he need to be baptized ‘right now’?” Take answers.
teach: Read Romans 6:3-11. Say: “‘Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.’ The Paschal Mystery is Christ’s passing from death to life: his Passion, death, Resurrection and Ascension. We share in it in Baptism. Going into the water is a burial; coming out is rising. The Church’s whole sacramental life flows from Christ’s Pasch. This is why the Easter Vigil is the great night of Baptisms.”

Say: “What does Baptism do? It forgives original sin and all personal sin. It makes us children of God, members of Christ and temples of the Holy Spirit. It incorporates us into the Church. It gives sanctifying grace and the theological virtues. It imprints an indelible character, which is why it cannot be repeated. The rite has signs: water, the sign of the cross, the oil of catechumens, the profession of faith, the white garment, the lighted candle. Infant Baptism: the Church has baptized infants since apostolic times (Acts 16:15, 33; 1 Corinthians 1:16 refer to ‘households’), on the basis of faith of the parents and godparents, as circumcision was done to infants. The parents promise to raise the child in the faith.”

Say: “Baptism of desire and blood: someone who dies for Christ before being baptized, or someone who desires Baptism but dies before receiving it, can be saved. Adult converts go through the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults (RCIA), receiving Baptism, Confirmation and Eucharist at the Easter Vigil. Baptism in other Christian communities is valid if done with water and the Trinitarian formula; so converts from other Christian groups are not rebaptized. We renew our promises at Easter: ‘Do you reject Satan? And all his works? And all his empty promises?’ In daily life, dying to sin means turning away from selfishness; rising means a new life of love. We make the Sign of the Cross with holy water as a reminder.”
ask: What does Baptism do? (Forgives sin; makes us children of God and members of the Church; gives grace.)
Why can Baptism be received only once? (It leaves an indelible mark.)
Why do we baptize infants? (Apostolic practice; faith of the parents and Church.)
practice: Create a flowchart of the rite of Baptism with all signs: Sign of the Cross, readings, anointing, blessing of the water, renunciation and profession of faith, pouring of water, chrism, white garment, candle.
Beside each, write what it means and the Romans 6 connection.
Write your own baptismal date and godparents, if known.
Renew your promises together.
script.close: Renew the baptismal promises. Bless yourselves with water. Send home: “Find your baptismal certificate or candle.”

tryit: Walk through the rite of Baptism.
Match each sign to Romans 6.
Renew your promises.
lessons.saintStory:
Philip was one of the seven deacons chosen in Jerusalem (Acts 6). After Stephen’s martyrdom, the persecution scattered the Christians, and Philip went to Samaria, where he preached and many believed.
An angel then told him to go south, on the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza. There he saw an Ethiopian official, the treasurer of Queen Candace, riding in his chariot, reading aloud from the prophet Isaiah. The Spirit said, “Go over and join this chariot.” Philip ran up and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” The man said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” and invited Philip to sit with him. The passage was Isaiah 53, “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter.” Philip began with that Scripture and told him the good news of Jesus.
As they went along, they came to some water. The Ethiopian said, “See, here is water! What is to prevent my being baptized?” They went down into the water and Philip baptized him. Then the Spirit carried Philip away, and the eunuch went on his way rejoicing.

lessons.title: The Eucharist: Christ’s sacrifice
lessons.idea: The Eucharist is Christ’s sacrifice made present: memorial, presence, sacrifice and banquet. The Mass is not a new sacrifice but the one sacrifice of Calvary made sacramentally present, in which we are united to Christ’s offering to the Father.
lessons.question: How is Mass a sacrifice?
lessons.activity: “Contrast misconceptions” (40 min). Students sort claims: “The Mass re-crucifies Christ” (false), “It’s only a meal” (incomplete), “The priest makes God come down” (misleading). Write the Catholic statement for each using CCC 1362–1367 and Hebrews 9–10. Role-play an explanation to a friend.
teach: The Eucharist is “the memorial of Christ’s Passover” (CCC 1362). Memorial (anamnesis) makes present the event (CCC 1363). “The sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice” (CCC 1367).
Hebrews insists Christ offered himself “once for all” (Hebrews 9:26–28; 10:10). The Mass does not repeat but re-presents it in an unbloody manner (CCC 1366–1367).
We are united to Christ’s offering, offering ourselves with him (CCC 1368). The Mass is offered for the living and the dead.
The Eucharist is also a banquet, the Lord’s Supper, whose fruits include union with Christ (CCC 1391–1397).
talk: How is the Mass a sacrifice?
quiz: The Mass is a “memorial” in the biblical sense, meaning…|A drama|A symbol|Making present a saving event (CCC 1363)|Remembering only|2|CCC 1363.
Hebrews 9–10 says Christ’s sacrifice is…|Repeated often|Offered once for all (CCC 1366–1367)|Symbolic|Incomplete|1|Hebrews 10:10.
The Church answers “the Mass re-crucifies Christ” by saying…|It is false|It is one sacrifice made sacramentally present, without repetition (CCC 1367)|It adds to Calvary|Yes|1|CCC 1367.
lessons.life: Offer yourself at the offertory.
lessons.saint: Pius X: the pope who welcomed children to Communion and urged frequent reception.
misc: “The Eucharist is only a meal of fellowship.”
lessons.mem: “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” (Luke 22:19)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What does ‘memorial’ mean for you?” (a monument, a birthday). In Scripture, a memorial makes a past saving event present (Exodus 12:14).
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain “memorial” and how the Mass is one sacrifice with Calvary.

script.open: Ask, “Why does the Mass include a meal, a story, a sacrifice, a song and a sending? Is it one thing or many? What is the Mass, in one sentence?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Mass makes present the Paschal Mystery. At the Last Supper, Jesus anticipated his death by giving his Body and Blood under bread and wine. On the cross, he offered himself. The Council of Trent said that in the Mass ‘that same Christ is contained and offered in an unbloody manner who offered himself once in a bloody manner on the altar of the cross.’ It’s not a new sacrifice nor a repetition. There is one sacrifice, and the Mass makes it present in every time and place. Hebrews teaches that Christ offered himself ‘once for all.’ (Hebrews 10:10) The Eucharistic Prayer’s anamnesis (remembrance) is not merely recalling but making present.”

Say: “The Eucharist has three dimensions. Sacrifice: Christ offers himself to the Father, and the Church offers with him and in him. This is why we say the priest offers the sacrifice ‘in persona Christi,’ and the people offer too. We offer ourselves: our work, joys, sufferings. Real presence: Christ is present under the appearances of bread and wine, body, blood, soul and divinity. ‘This is my body.’ Communion: we receive him, and are united with him and one another. Paul: ‘Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.’ (1 Corinthians 10:17) The Church makes the Eucharist and the Eucharist makes the Church.”

Say: “Related teaching. Transubstantiation: the substance of bread and wine is changed into the substance of Christ’s body and blood, while the appearances remain. Trent used this term. Eucharistic worship outside Mass: the reserved Sacrament, adoration, Benediction, processions. Obligation: Catholics must attend Mass on Sundays and holy days, and receive Communion at least once a year at Easter. Worthy reception requires the state of grace, a one-hour fast, and reverence. Intercommunion: because Communion signifies full unity in faith, the Church normally reserves Communion to Catholics, with exceptions for Orthodox and others in special cases. The Church also reveres the Eucharist as the ‘source and summit of the Christian life.’ A mature Catholic lives from the Mass.”
ask: Is the Mass a new sacrifice? (No; it makes the one sacrifice of Calvary present.)
What are the three dimensions? (Sacrifice, real presence, communion.)
What is transubstantiation? (The substance changes; the appearances remain.)
practice: Make a three-column table: Sacrifice, Presence, Communion.
Under each, write the parts of the Mass that show it, a Scripture text, and what it asks of me.
Write a prayer to say before Mass.
Attend Mass this week with one intention in mind.
script.close: Pray the Anima Christi. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Prepare for Sunday Mass by reading the Gospel.”

tryit: List the Eucharist’s three dimensions.
Match each to a part of the Mass.
Write what it asks of the participant.
lessons.saintStory:
Giuseppe Sarto was born in 1835 in a poor village in northern Italy, the son of a postman and seamstress. He became a priest, a pastor, a bishop and a cardinal-patriarch of Venice. When he went to Rome for the conclave of 1903, he bought a round-trip ticket, expecting to return. Instead, he was elected pope, Pius X. He said, “I was born poor, I lived poor, I will die poor.”
He made the Eucharist central. In 1905 he encouraged frequent and even daily Communion, which had become rare because of an excessive sense of unworthiness. In 1910, in the decree Quam Singulari, he lowered the age for First Communion to about seven, the age of reason, so that children could receive Jesus early. He also restored Gregorian chant to the liturgy, promoted the study of the Catechism, and reformed the Roman Curia and canon law.
He died in 1914, shortly after the outbreak of World War I, and was canonized in 1954.

lessons.title: Prayer and Christian hope
lessons.idea: Christian hope is a theological virtue by which we desire heaven and trust in God’s promises. It sustains prayer, especially in suffering, and is rooted in the Resurrection. “In this hope we were saved.”
lessons.question: What is hope?
lessons.activity: “Write a hope letter” (35 min). Students write a letter to someone who is struggling (or to their future selves) that names real difficulty, shares reasons for hope from Scripture (Romans 8:28; Jeremiah 29:11), and offers a prayer. Seal or share with permission.
teach: Hope is “the theological virtue by which we desire the kingdom of heaven and eternal life as our happiness, placing our trust in Christ’s promises” (CCC 1817). It guards against discouragement and presumption (CCC 2090–2092).
Prayer is the school of hope (CCC 1820, 2657–2658). Romans 8 shows the Spirit helping us in weakness. Mary and the saints model hope.
Christian hope does not deny suffering; it sees it in light of the Resurrection (CCC 1521, 1817–1821). Spe Salvi (Benedict XVI) develops this.
Teach students that hope is shared and active.
talk: How does hope differ from optimism?
quiz: Christian hope differs from optimism because it…|Ignores suffering|Is a mood|Expects comfort|Trusts God’s promises and desires eternal life (CCC 1817)|3|CCC 1817.
The two sins against hope are…|Anger and envy|Pride and vanity|Gluttony and sloth|Despair and presumption (CCC 2091–2092)|3|CCC 2091–2092.
Prayer helps hope by…|Silence|Replacing action|Keeping us in contact with the God who promises (CCC 2657–2658)|Telling us the future|2|CCC 2657–2658.
lessons.life: Write a letter of hope to your future self.
lessons.saint: Cardinal Nguyễn Văn Thuận: an archbishop who spent thirteen years in prison and never lost hope.
misc: “Hope means everything will go my way.”
lessons.mem: “For in this hope we were saved.” (Romans 8:24)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do you do when you need hope?” Read Romans 8:24–25: “Hope that is seen is not hope.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to define hope and name two ways prayer nourishes it.

script.open: Say, “Imagine being alone in a room with no windows for a year. What would you do to keep your mind and spirit alive? What would you hold on to?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Christian hope is the theological virtue by which we desire the Kingdom of heaven and eternal life as our happiness, trusting in Christ’s promises and relying not on our own strength but on the help of the Holy Spirit. (CCC 1817) It is not optimism, a feeling that things will turn out okay. It is trust in God who has already won in Christ. Hebrews 6:19: ‘We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul.’ The Paschal Mystery gives the shape: the cross leads to the Resurrection. Romans 8:24: ‘In this hope we were saved.’ Pope Benedict XVI’s encyclical Spe Salvi (2007) says, ‘The one who has hope lives differently.’”

Say: “Hope is nourished by prayer. The Catechism calls prayer ‘the school of hope.’ Prayer is the raising of the mind and heart to God. We pray with vocal prayer, meditation and contemplation. We pray with the Psalms, the Our Father, and the Rosary. We pray in the Liturgy of the Hours. We pray with silence and Scripture. A simple daily rhythm: morning offering; grace at meals; some Scripture or a psalm; an Examen in the evening; and a short night prayer. In the Our Father, the seven petitions sum up all hope. In suffering, prayer is a lifeline.”

Say: “The Church’s hope is also about the last things. Death: the end of earthly life; the soul is judged. Heaven: eternal life with God, the beatific vision, seeing God face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). Purgatory: purification. Hell: the state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God, a real possibility because we are free. Final resurrection: our bodies will be raised. New creation: ‘a new heaven and a new earth.’ We live in the ‘already, but not yet.’ Cardinal Thuận wrote, ‘I will not wait. I will live the present moment and fill it to the brim with love.’ Christian hope shapes how we face suffering and death: with prayer and peace. The Church’s rites for the dying, Viaticum and the Anointing, give strength.”
ask: What is Christian hope? (Trust in God’s promise of eternal life through Christ.)
What is the beatific vision? (Seeing God face to face in heaven.)
How does prayer nourish hope? (It keeps us in relationship with God.)
practice: Design a daily prayer rhythm: morning, midday, evening, night.
Include at least four elements (Morning Offering, Scripture, grace, Examen).
List three sources of hope that you can reach in a hard time.
Share your rhythm with a partner, and commit to trying it for a week.
script.close: Pray the Act of Hope together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Follow your daily prayer plan for a week.”

tryit: Write a plan for a daily prayer rhythm.
Include the Examen and Scripture.
List a source of hope in hard times.
lessons.saintStory:
Francis Xavier Nguyễn Văn Thuận was born in 1928 in Vietnam, a family with deep Catholic roots. He became a priest, then bishop of Nha Trang. In April 1975, just days before the fall of Saigon, Pope Paul VI named him coadjutor archbishop of Saigon. The Communists took over, and he was arrested, accused of conspiring with foreign powers. He was imprisoned for thirteen years, nine of them in solitary confinement.
He was kept in a cell without a window; the light was kept on all the time. He decided to use each day to love. He secretly celebrated Mass with three drops of wine and a drop of water in the palm of his hand, and a piece of bread, which friends smuggled in as medicine for stomach ache. He made a cross from scraps of wood and wire. His guards, who at first were forbidden to talk to him, became his friends; he taught them French and Latin, and some began to pray.
Released in 1988, he was exiled in 1991, and became a cardinal in 2001 and worked at the Vatican on justice and peace. He wrote The Road of Hope and Testimony of Hope. He died in 2002.
