units.eq: What does the Church teach about life and love, and why?

lessons.title: Abortion and the dignity of the unborn
lessons.idea: Every human life is a gift from conception to natural death, so direct abortion is gravely wrong. The Church also calls us to love and help mothers and children.
lessons.question: How does the Church answer the hardest cases?
lessons.activity: Research a local pregnancy-help center and what it offers.
teach: Sensitive topic: some students have lived through it. Teach clearly, with compassion, and give them room to step out.

Human life begins at conception and must be protected (CCC 2270). “Direct abortion… is gravely contrary to the moral law” (CCC 2271). The Church treats ending an unborn life as a very grave wrong, and the Church’s law attaches excommunication to those who procure it (CCC 2272), with the hope of mercy through Confession.

The Church recognizes real fear, poverty, abandonment and difficult pregnancies, including after rape. Teaching that the child has dignity never means leaving the mother alone: support, adoption and care (CCC 2367).

Treatments needed to save a mother’s life that unintentionally result in the death of her unborn child, for example for a cancer or an ectopic pregnancy, are not “direct abortion.” Healing after abortion is real: Project Rachel and Rachel’s Vineyard.
talk: What are the best ways a community can support a pregnant teenager?
Why does the Church link the dignity of the unborn with the dignity of the poor and the sick?
How can we speak about this without shaming people?
quiz: What does CCC 2270 teach about human life?|Personhood is decided by law|It depends on age|It must be respected and protected from conception|Life begins at birth|2|CCC 2270.
The sacrament that offers forgiveness and healing after abortion is…|Reconciliation (Confession)|Anointing of the Sick only|Holy Orders|Confirmation|0|CCC 1446, 2272.

A treatment to save a mother’s life that indirectly results in the death of her unborn child is…|Not considered direct abortion|Required to be kept secret|Prohibited as any surgery|Always the same as abortion|0|The principle of double effect.
lessons.life: Pray the Rosary for mothers and children, or collect supplies for a pregnancy-help center.
lessons.saint: Margaret of Castello: a child abandoned for her disabilities, who became a Dominican sister and a comforter of others.
misc: “The Church cares about babies only before they are born.”
“The Church cannot forgive someone who has had an abortion.”
lessons.mem: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you.” (Jeremiah 1:5)
lessons.hook: Say that some students in the room may have lived through this, and that the aim is truth with compassion. Anyone may step out.
lessons.assess: Ask students to state the Church’s teaching and name three ways to support women and families in crisis.

script.open: Say gently and clearly, “This lesson is on one of the most painful and divisive issues of our time. We will speak with truth and compassion. Some of you may have personal experiences. Nobody here will be judged. Let’s start with the question: what makes a human being valuable?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Catholic Church teaches that human life is sacred and must be respected from the moment of conception. The Catechism: ‘Human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception. From the first moment of his existence, a human being must be recognized as having the rights of a person—among which is the inviolable right of every innocent being to life.’ (CCC 2270) The reasons: Biblical: ‘Before I formed you in the womb I knew you.’ (Jeremiah 1:5; Psalm 139:13-16; Luke 1:41-44, John the Baptist leaps in the womb). Biological: at conception a new, genetically distinct human organism begins. Philosophical: personhood doesn’t depend on size, stage, ability, or dependence. The Didache, from about AD 100: ‘You shall not kill a child by abortion.’”

Say: “Direct abortion, the deliberate termination of a pregnancy, is gravely wrong. The Church also attaches the penalty of excommunication to those who procure a completed abortion, to emphasize the gravity and to help people see their need for repentance (CCC 2272). The Church distinguishes this from medical treatment to save a mother’s life that has the unintended effect of ending the pregnancy (the principle of double effect). Examples: removing a cancerous uterus or treating an ectopic pregnancy, where the aim is to save the mother and not to end the child’s life. The Church also condemns embryonic stem-cell research that destroys embryos, and in vitro fertilization that creates and discards embryos. In 2022, the U.S. Supreme Court in Dobbs overturned Roe v. Wade, returning the question to the states.”

Say: “The Church’s teaching is joined with compassion. Many women who choose abortion feel pressured, afraid or abandoned. The Church calls for support. Pregnancy resource centers provide free medical help, counseling, diapers and housing. Adoption is a generous option. Healing is available for those who have had abortions: the Church teaches that God’s mercy is greater than any sin, and the sacrament of Reconciliation is available. Projects such as Project Rachel and Rachel’s Vineyard offer counseling and retreats. What about hard cases? Pregnancy from rape: the Church acknowledges the terrible suffering of the woman and urges compassion and care; the child is innocent and also a victim. A diagnosis of disability: Margaret of Castello shows the worth of a life beyond ability. The Church’s message: love both. ‘Choose life, that you and your descendants may live.’ (Deuteronomy 30:19)”
ask: What does the Church teach about when life begins? (From conception.)
What is the principle of double effect? (Allows treatment that saves the mother even if it unintentionally ends the pregnancy.)
What help does the Church offer after an abortion? (Mercy in Reconciliation, and healing ministries.)
practice: Make two columns: “Reasons the Church gives” and “Ways to help mothers and children.”
Fill in with at least five items each.
Choose one way to help locally (a pregnancy center, a diaper drive, a prayer group).
Write a prayer for mothers, children and those who have suffered through abortion.
script.close: Pray the Hail Mary for mothers and unborn children. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “If you or someone you know needs help, speak with a trusted adult or priest.”

tryit: List the Church’s reasons for protecting the unborn.
List the help she offers to mothers.
Plan one act of support.
lessons.saintStory:
Margaret was born in 1287 in Metola, Italy, to a nobleman and his wife. She was born blind, with a curved spine and a limp, and was very small. Her parents, ashamed of her, hid her away for years in a small room. When she was six, they took her to a shrine, and hoping for a cure, prayed. No miracle came. They left her there and went home.
Margaret was abandoned in a strange town, and fended for herself as a beggar. Eventually, poor families took her in. She was cheerful and prayed constantly, and taught the children the Psalms, which she had learned by heart. She joined the Dominican laity, and visited prisoners and the sick. People noticed how joyful she was.
She died at thirty-three, in 1320. An autopsy was said to reveal three small stones in her heart, each bearing a holy image. In 2021 Pope Francis extended her veneration to the whole Church as a saint. She is invoked as a patron of the unborn and disabled.

lessons.title: Contraception, NFP and Humanae Vitae
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that married love is meant to be total and open to life, so it asks couples to avoid artificial contraception and to practice natural family planning when they have serious reasons to space births.
lessons.question: Why does the Church say no to the pill?
lessons.activity: Read an excerpt from Humanae Vitae 12 and 14 with a partner and summarize in your own words.
teach: Sensitive topic: aim for clarity and respect; this is a teaching many Catholics reject or have never heard.

The Catechism teaches that the marital act has two meanings, unitive and procreative, which should not be separated (CCC 2366; Humanae Vitae 12, Paul VI, 1968). Contraception is therefore not permitted (CCC 2370).
The Church also affirms responsible parenthood (CCC 2368). Spouses with serious reasons may use natural family planning, which uses the body’s natural signs, not drugs or devices.

Not all hormonal treatments are always the same: medicines used to treat illness are a different question. Many couples find NFP demanding and some find it life-giving; the Church acknowledges hardship and offers support, mercy and Confession rather than condemnation.
talk: What do you think “total self-giving” means in a marriage?
Why might Paul VI’s teaching in 1968 have been so controversial?
What is the difference between NFP and contraception, according to the Church?
quiz: Humanae Vitae was written by…|Pope Paul VI|Pope Francis|Pope John XXIII|Pope Pius XII|0|1968.
The two meanings of the marital act are…|Legal and social|Private and public|Physical and emotional only|Unitive and procreative|3|CCC 2366.
The Church allows couples with serious reasons to…|Use any method|Space births using natural family planning|Refuse marriage|Never plan families|1|CCC 2368, 2370.
lessons.life: Pray for engaged and married couples you know.
lessons.saint: Zélie and Louis Martin: parents of Thérèse, who raised nine children with faith and love.
misc: “The Church wants couples to have as many children as possible.”
lessons.mem: “Be fruitful and multiply.” (Genesis 1:28)
lessons.hook: Acknowledge that many Catholics have never heard this teaching, and that the aim is to understand it, not to shame anyone.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the Church’s teaching in their own words and describe how NFP differs from contraception.

script.open: Ask, “What do you think marriage is for? List purposes.” Write them. Circle “love” and “children.” Ask, “Can these be separated? Should they be?”
teach: Say: “Catholic teaching on marriage is that it is a covenant between a man and a woman, ordered to the good of the spouses and the procreation and education of children. These are the two ‘ends,’ or meanings, of marriage: the unitive (love) and the procreative (children). Humanae Vitae (1968), Pope Paul VI’s encyclical, taught that ‘each and every marriage act must remain open to the transmission of life.’ (HV 11) This follows from the inseparable connection between the unitive and procreative meanings of the marital act. It does not mean that every act produces a child, but that couples should not deliberately frustrate it.”

Say: “Contraception is any action before, during or after intercourse intended to prevent procreation. The Church teaches that it is morally wrong. Reasons: it separates the unitive and procreative meanings that God joined. It says to your spouse, ‘I give you all of me except my fertility.’ It reduces the person to an object to be used. Paul VI predicted consequences: a general lowering of moral standards, marital infidelity, loss of respect for women, and governments imposing birth control. Many point to the sexual revolution as evidence. The Church holds that it’s about total self-giving: marriage is a gift of self. Critics argue the teaching is unrealistic; surveys show most Catholics disagree. The Church doesn’t decide by polls, but she must explain it well.”

Say: “Responsible parenthood. The Church doesn’t demand maximal numbers of children. Couples can space births or limit family size for serious reasons (health, finances, emotional readiness). They may use Natural Family Planning (NFP): methods based on observing a woman’s natural signs of fertility (cervical mucus, temperature) and abstaining during fertile times if avoiding pregnancy. NFP is different from the old calendar rhythm method. Modern methods such as Creighton, Billings and Symptothermal are more than 95-99 percent effective with correct use in studies. The difference: contraception acts against fertility; NFP cooperates with it. NFP requires communication, self-control and cooperation. Many couples report greater intimacy. NFP is also used to achieve pregnancy and for women’s health. Zélie and Louis show a family’s joy and cost: their trust in God sustained them.”
ask: What are the two meanings of marriage? (Unitive and procreative.)
What does NFP do? (Uses natural signs of fertility to space births, cooperating with fertility.)
Does the Church require couples to have as many children as possible? (No; responsible parenthood allows spacing for serious reasons.)
practice: Lay out HV’s reasoning in four steps: marriage’s two meanings; their inseparable connection; therefore, no deliberate frustration; therefore NFP.
Write the strongest objection and a reply.
Compare NFP and contraception in a chart.
Write one question you would like to ask a married couple about the teaching.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, bless every married couple and every family.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask a married couple what marriage has taught them.”

tryit: Lay out the reasoning of Humanae Vitae.
Compare methods.
Write one question and a reply.
lessons.saintStory:
Louis Martin was a watchmaker and Zélie Guérin a lacemaker in Alençon, France. Each had once tried to enter religious life and been refused. They met in 1858 and married three months later. Louis proposed that they live as brother and sister, but a confessor advised them to open themselves to children. They had nine children between 1860 and 1873. Four died in infancy or childhood, which devastated them. Five daughters survived, and all became nuns, including Thérèse of Lisieux.
They went to Mass daily, kept the fast, and prayed together. Zélie ran a successful lace business, while caring for children and writing many letters, which survive. In 1877, she died of breast cancer, at forty-five. Louis moved the family to Lisieux and raised the girls. Later he suffered strokes and dementia and was placed in a hospital, which was a great humiliation, and he died in 1894.
In 2015, Pope Francis canonized them, the first married couple canonized together. Their story shows marriage as a path to holiness.

lessons.title: Chastity: what is it for?
lessons.idea: Chastity is the virtue that lets us love well with our whole person. The Church teaches that sexual intimacy belongs to marriage and that every person is called to chastity in their state of life.
lessons.question: Is chastity just about saying no?
lessons.activity: Write a personal rule of life for friendships, screens and dating.
teach: Chastity is about integrating sexuality in the person, not repressing it (CCC 2337). Everyone, married, single or celibate, is called to chastity (CCC 2348–2349).

The Church teaches that sexual intimacy is for the permanent, faithful, fruitful bond of marriage and that fornication, pornography and lust fall short of love (CCC 2351–2356). Pornography does serious harm to the person and to relationships (CCC 2354).
Teens face real pressure and shame. The Church offers a vision of dignity and a path of mercy: Confession, prayer, good friends, honesty, healthy boundaries. Failure is not final.
Chastity is a virtue that grows with practice, like any other. It is not the same as shame or silence about the body.
talk: What pressures do teens face about love and the body?
Why does the Church say chastity is about love?
What habits help someone to grow in this virtue?

Who is called to chastity?|Only the unmarried|Only girls|Everyone, in their own state of life|Only priests|2|CCC 2348.

lessons.life: Choose one habit this week that protects your heart, such as a screen boundary or an evening prayer.
lessons.saint: Maria Goretti: a girl who chose to die rather than sin, and whose attacker was converted by her forgiveness.
misc: “The Church thinks the body and sex are dirty.”
“Chastity means never being close to anyone.”
lessons.mem: “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Corinthians 6:19)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is chastity about saying no, or about saying yes to something?” Take answers.
lessons.assess: Ask students to define chastity and write a personal rule for friendships and screens.

script.open: Be calm and respectful. Say, “This is about a beautiful topic that society often gets wrong. Let’s begin with a question: what is the opposite of love? Is it hate?” Take answers. “Karol Wojtyła, later Pope John Paul II, said the opposite of love is use.”
teach: Say: “The Church teaches that sexuality is a gift of God, good and holy, meant for love and life within marriage. The Catechism: ‘Chastity means the successful integration of sexuality within the person and thereby the inner unity of man in his bodily and spiritual being.’ (CCC 2337) Chastity is not repression; it’s self-mastery for the sake of love. It is a virtue for everyone: single people, married people, priests and religious, each according to their state. Married chastity means fidelity. For the unmarried, chastity means abstaining from sexual relations. In dating, it means respecting each other’s dignity and the meaning of the body.”

Say: “John Paul II developed this in his Theology of the Body (1979-84). The body expresses the person; it has a ‘nuptial meaning,’ the capacity to express love by self-gift. Sex is a total gift of self, ‘I am yours, completely, permanently,’ which is why it belongs to marriage. Outside that, it says something false with the body. He wrote in Love and Responsibility that a person is never to be used merely as a means. Sins against chastity include lust, masturbation, fornication, pornography, prostitution, rape and homosexual acts. Pornography is gravely harmful: it reduces persons to objects, can be addictive, and distorts how we see others. Most people struggle with these things; the Church teaches that God’s mercy is greater, that Confession heals, and that growth in chastity is possible with grace.”

Say: “What about people with same-sex attraction? The Catechism teaches that homosexual acts are not in accord with the natural law, but that persons with homosexual tendencies ‘must be accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity. Every sign of unjust discrimination in their regard should be avoided.’ (CCC 2358) They are called to chastity, like everyone. Practical help: pray; frequent Confession and Mass; avoid occasions of sin (what you watch, who you are alone with); set clear limits in dating; modesty in dress and speech as respect for self and others; friendships; talking to a trusted adult. Chastity and purity are not just about avoiding sin but about positive love. ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.’ (Matthew 5:8)”
ask: What is chastity? (Integrating sexuality in the person for the sake of love, according to one’s state.)
What did John Paul II say is the opposite of love? (Use.)
How does the Church say we should treat persons with same-sex attraction? (With respect, compassion and sensitivity; no unjust discrimination.)
practice: Draw a line from “use” to “love” and place examples along it: treating a date as a trophy, texting a kind note, pressuring a partner, waiting, pornography, honoring a friend.
Write your own definition of chastity in your own words.
Write a short personal commitment and one step to keep it: boundaries, friends, screen habits.
Keep it private or share with a trusted adult.
script.close: Pray: “Create in me a clean heart, O God.” (Psalm 51:10.) Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Talk with a trusted adult or priest about any questions.”

tryit: Define chastity in your own words.
Sort actions into respect and use.
Write your commitment.
lessons.saintStory:
Maria Goretti was born in 1890 in Italy, to a poor farming family. When she was nine, her father died of malaria, and the family moved to work on a farm with another family, the Serenellis. Maria cooked, cleaned and cared for her younger siblings while her mother worked in the fields. She was devout, and prepared for First Communion at eleven.
Alessandro Serenelli, a young man of eighteen, began pressing her for sexual favors. She refused. On July 5, 1902, when they were alone in the house, he attacked her. She resisted, crying, “No! It is a sin! God does not want it!” He stabbed her fourteen times. She died the next day in the hospital. Before dying, she forgave him and said she wanted him in heaven with her.
Alessandro spent twenty-seven years in prison, unrepentant. Then he had a dream in which Maria offered him lilies. He repented and was released. He asked Maria’s mother for forgiveness, and she forgave him. In 1950, Alessandro stood with Maria’s mother at Maria’s canonization. He ended his life as a lay brother with the Capuchins.
